name: North Ridge
beta: The route comprises three ridge sections separated by deep notches. The lower section is mostly class 2-4 terrain, commonly simul-climbed, staying just on the east side of the crest (harder climbing results if the crest itself is followed). After descending to the second notch, two 5.8 pitches (a dirty 5.8 chimney and a 5.8 crack pitch) lead toward the summit, separated by class 2-3 sections, with large detached blocks making protection difficult in places. A gendarme partway up offers the route's best technical climbing directly, or can be bypassed via a ~75-ft rappel to easier terrain west of the ridge.
overview: Sherpa's North Ridge is a longer, more sustained alpine rock route than the south-side ridges, climbing directly above the Sherpa-Argonaut basin with 4th/5th-class scrambling low on the ridge and several sustained 5.7-5.8 pitches higher up, just left (east) of the crest. It's a full alpine day (around 10 hours) requiring real rope-management skill, since much of the route is simul-climbed or short-roped rather than broken into clean pitches.

current.approach: The North Ridge is most commonly approached from the north via the Stuart Lake Trailhead (reached by Icicle Creek Road/Eightmile Creek Road out of Leavenworth). Follow the Stuart Lake Trail (#1599) along Mountaineer Creek roughly 3.5-4 miles, climbing gently through forest. Before reaching Stuart/Colchuck Lake, leave the maintained trail, cross Mountaineer Creek, and pick up a boot path/cairned route that climbs talus benches on the slope west of the creek, staying a couple hundred feet above the trees before dropping back toward the creek, aiming for the Argonaut-Sherpa basin. Around 5,800 ft, the route steepens into sustained loose talus leading up to the base of the North Ridge proper (~7,000 ft), a roughly 1,500-ft-tall rock feature capped by the 8,630-ft summit. At the base, contour and work climber's-right to a lower notch, where easy slabs can be scrambled before roping up. (A southern approach via Longs Pass and Ingalls Creek to Mountaineer Creek is also possible but is a longer, less direct line to this specific route.) Water is available at Mountaineer Creek but is limited higher on the talus approach - carry enough for the day. The talus benches and loose approach gully are the main hazards; expect a long, sustained boulder-hop that is more tedious than technical.
approach_variant_names: Mountaineer Creek to the Sherpa-Argonaut basin, then talus west-northwest to the lower notch
current.descent: Descent is not a reversal of the North Ridge and is considered the trickiest part of the route. From the summit, downclimb/scramble a short distance to an established rappel station just west of the true summit - the top anchor of the standard West Ridge route - and make a short rappel (roughly 25-30 ft/one short pitch) down into a gully southwest of the summit. A second, shorter rappel (about 20 ft, off a slung boulder) follows; this one is optional and can be downclimbed at low 5th class by confident parties. Some parties describe this stage as two ~25m rappels rather than two short single-pitch raps, so treat the exact length as variable and carry a 50-60m rope to cover either version. Below the rappels, the terrain eases from sustained class 3 (roughly the first 500 ft) to class 2; continue southeast across loose rocky ribs and gullies, staying low to avoid cliff bands, toward the Sherpa-Argonaut saddle. The final ~1,000 ft down to treeline from the saddle is the descent's crux - loose rock only barely held in place by dirt and sand - so move carefully and stay alert for parties below. From the basin, either retrace the approach out via Mountaineer Creek and the Stuart Lake Trail to the north trailhead, or cross south to Ingalls Creek and over Longs Pass, depending on where your car is staged.
current.detailed_rack: Single rack through hand size with a set of nuts; light snow kit for the approach early season.
current.pro_needs: Medium alpine rack; axe/crampons if approach snow lingers.

name: West Ridge
beta: From the col between Mount Stuart and Sherpa Peak, ascend the ridge generally trending climber's left. With a 60m rope you can reach the first belay in a cave-like feature with a platform large enough for several climbers; the crux is the crack leading out of the cave (rated 5.4-5.5). A second pitch leads to another anchor, after which a short 4th-class scramble gains the notoriously airy summit block. Descent is about four rappels down the ascent line, three single-rope and a final double-rope rappel to the west notch.
overview: Sherpa Peak's West Ridge is the classic, most-traveled line up this Stuart Range spire east of Mount Stuart, mixing a long Class 4 ridge scramble with roughly five short pitches of low-5th-class climbing to a 5.4 crux below the summit ridge. Most parties tag the sub-summit and treat the adjacent Sherpa Balanced Rock obelisk (5.7, shoulder-stand + friction) as an optional bonus.

current.approach: From the Esmeralda Basin/Longs Pass Trailhead (end of Teanaway River Road/FS-9737, ~4,300 ft), take the Longs Pass Trail (#1229) roughly 2.3 miles and about 2,300 ft of gain to Longs Pass (~6,200 ft), a broad open saddle. From the pass, drop steeply down the north side (a boot path, with snow fingers usable for glissading in early season) about 1,300-1,400 ft to the Ingalls Creek drainage (~4,800 ft). Ford or rock-hop Ingalls Creek (can run high with early-season snowmelt) and pick up the Ingalls Creek Trail, following it right (east) about a half to full mile to the Beverly-Turnpike Trail junction. Leave the maintained trail here for a boot/climbers' path (sometimes called the "tapeworm trail") that switchbacks up through timber and brush before opening into meadow beneath Sherpa and Argonaut Peaks. Gain the rounded rib dividing the Cascadian Couloir drainage from the basin under Sherpa, then contour around 5,800 ft into the snow-holding basin below the West Ridge; kick steps up final snow/talus slopes to a common bivy/base-camp shelf around 7,400 ft (a flat table-rock area) or continue straight to the ridge base. Total gain from the car to the base of technical climbing runs roughly 3,400-4,700 ft depending on whether you camp or go car-to-car, with 6-7 hours of hiking typical for the one-way approach. Water is available at Ingalls Creek and from snowmelt in the upper basin in season; the brushy bushwhack down to Ingalls Creek and the long boulder/talus field beneath Sherpa are the main route-finding and stamina cruxes of the approach.
approach_variant_names: Esmeralda TH over Longs Pass and up from Ingalls Creek
current.descent: The standard descent reverses the West Ridge using a sequence of rappels rather than downclimbing the whole route. From the summit area, two single-rope rappels lead down past the crux (5.4-5.6) pitch to a short 3rd-class scramble; this is followed by another single-rope rappel and then a longer double-rope rappel (two ropes joined, or a single 60m doubled) that returns you to the west notch below the technical climbing. Anchors are a mix of fixed slings around horns and flakes; most are solid (slings around big, well-set flakes/horns), but at least one reported station was backed by a sketchy bundle of slings wrapped around a few small loose rocks next to the actual load-bearing horn - inspect and back up questionable tat with your own gear. Some parties skip the last downclimb and instead rappel directly down the loose, dirty gully from the notch. Bring a 60m rope (or two ropes for the double-rope stretch) and extra slings/cord to replace weathered anchors. From the notch, descend scree/talus and boot path back into the basin (glissading is possible on lingering snow) to camp, then reverse the approach over Longs Pass to the trailhead. Total rappel count is commonly described as four stations (two singles, a scramble, one more single, then one double-rope rappel); some parties count this as three rappels depending on how stations are combined, so expect 3-4 total.
current.detailed_rack: A light rack of cams to 2 inches, a set of nuts, several slings for horns, and a 60m rope to protect the summit block and rappel off it.
current.pro_needs: Protection is adequate on the short crux moves and the summit block, but most of the ridge is unprotected scrambling. Comfort on exposed terrain is key.
bivy: Table Rock bivy, upper Sherpa basin
Beverly and De Roux campgrounds and the North Fork Teanaway roadside camps
Ingalls Creek valley camps below the Sherpa and Argonaut south sides

name: Sidewinder
beta: Good feet throughout with one pumpy crux section that loads the arms; the difficulty here is more mental than physical since bolts are spaced roughly every four feet. The basalt climbs differently than Pinto Rock's typical knobby welded tuff, with a character closer to Exit 38. Best cleaned by the second since it's a lateral traverse.
overview: A slightly overhanging, bolt-protected traverse rightward (east) along a lichen-stained basalt band on Pinto Rock's north side, ending at a chain anchor near a roof.

current.approach: From Randle, WA on US Hwy 12: head south on SR 131, then follow NF-25 (Forest Road 25) for 19.2 miles; just past milepost 21, turn left at the sign for Mosquito Meadows onto NF-28 and follow it 2.7 miles; turn left onto NF-77 (rough gravel, drive slowly) for about 2 miles until Pinto Rock comes into view at a large pullout. An evident use trail leads north from the pullout to the base of the formation (~0.3 mi/0.47 km). For the North Side wall specifically, either hike around the formation's east side to the base, or summit via the standard trail/scramble and rappel the fixed rings, which meet the route partway.
current.descent: From the anchor at the end of the traverse, lower back to the base on a single rope (~60 ft). Many parties instead keep the rope through the anchor, lower to the roof lip, and set up a toprope on the adjacent Top Gun before finally lowering all the way to the ground.
current.detailed_rack: Sport rack: 10-12 quickdraws (bolts roughly every 4 ft over the 60 ft pitch) plus draws for the chain anchor; a 60m rope is sufficient for the lower.
current.pro_needs: Fully bolted; no trad gear needed. Bring at least 10-12 quickdraws.
current.rope_note: Single-pitch, slightly overhung sport route, bolts every ~4ft; lower from chains (anchor also used to toprope Top Gun).

name: Northeast Ridge
beta: Approach as for the Silver Star Glacier route to gain the glacier, then break off toward the northeast side of the west summit to climb the ridge/face directly rather than finishing via the standard scramble line. Beckey's 1952 party made the first recorded ascent of the west summit via this general northeast aspect from the glacier.
overview: A technical rock line up the west summit's northeast aspect, reached via the Silver Star Glacier; more sustained than the standard glacier route but far less documented.

current.approach: Same as the Silver Star Glacier route to Burgundy Col and onto the glacier (see that route for full trailhead-to-glacier detail), then trend toward the northeast side of the west summit.
approach_variant_names: SR-20 pullout, Burgundy Creek climbers' trail, the Bench, Burgundy Col
Silver Star Creek from the north
current.descent: Reverse via the glacier and Burgundy Col.
current.detailed_rack: A standard alpine rock rack plus glacier travel gear for the approach.
bivy: Burgundy Creek bench camp — west side
Burgundy Col high camp — west side, the Wine Spires
Upper scree benches below Burgundy Col — west side

name: West Face Couloir
beta: Start up the descent gully used for Gato Negro on adjacent Whine Spire, then follow the couloir; the first obstacle is a chockstone going at M2-3, followed by simulclimbing to a rightward fork and a crux chockstone requiring M4 climbing with minimal to no protection.
overview: An extended snow-and-ice couloir on Silver Star's western face, climbing to the west summit with a hard mixed chockstone crux.

current.approach: Approach via the Gato Negro descent gully on Whine Spire; 2-3 hours, snowshoes recommended in early-season snow.
current.descent: From the west summit, traverse/descend to join the Silver Star Glacier route and follow it back over Burgundy Col to the approach trail.
current.detailed_rack: Short rope, light alpine rack, and stubby ice screws.
current.pro_needs: The crux chockstone requires M4 mixed climbing with minimal to no protection; overall the route is lightly protected.

name: North Face
beta: From a col south of Sinister, descend onto the Chickamin Glacier and traverse to the base of the north face at its lowest point. Climb a direct line up the consistent 45-50 degree névé and ice, deviating only briefly to skirt the bergschrund, until the angle eases near the top and a short rock/snow scramble leads to the summit.
overview: A sustained 45-50 degree névé/ice face rising directly to the summit off the Chickamin Glacier — a striking, moderate (NCCS Grade II) alpine snow/ice line and one of the more scenic technical routes along the Ptarmigan Traverse.

current.approach: Follow the same multi-day approach as the Southwest Route to a high camp on Itswoot Ridge or near the Dome Glacier, then continue over the Dome-Chickamin Glacier col (~8,500 ft) and descend onto the Chickamin Glacier, traversing beneath Sinister's north side to reach the base of the face. The original 1980 first ascent instead approached from the Blizzard-Gunsight col, traversing the Chickamin Glacier from the west. The Downey Creek trail grows muddy, brushy and tangled with deadfall toward Bachelor Creek, then stays rooty and slick for hours until the basin below the ridge.
approach_variant_names: Downey Creek and Bachelor Creek to the ridge camp, then across onto the northern icefield
From the col to the west, traversing the icefield from that side
current.descent: Most parties downclimb the moderating upper snow slopes and pick an easier walk-off line (often via the west ridge) rather than reverse the full face; the line has also been skied. Return via the Chickamin and Dome Glaciers to Itswoot Ridge and out the Bachelor Creek/Downey Creek trails.
current.detailed_rack: A rack of 4-6 ice screws, 2-3 snow pickets, and a 60m rope for the sustained 45-50 degree névé/ice face; many parties simul-climb the consistent-angle slope with occasional running protection, saving belayed pitches for the bergschrund crossing near the base.
current.pro_needs: Ice screws and pickets for the sustained snow/ice face, plus standard glacier-travel protection (pickets, crevasse-rescue kit) for the Dome/Chickamin Glacier approach.
bivy: Dome Glacier and Dome-Chickamin col high bivouacs
Bachelor Creek forest and meadow camps

name: Southwest Route
beta: Approach via Downey Creek Trail to high camp at Cub Lake or Itswoot Ridge (5,400-6,400 ft). Traverse Chickamin Glacier to Dome-Sinister col at approximately 8,450 feet. Contour around Sinister's south side via easy snowfield, then climb a prominent loose gully (Class 3, loose rock) to the ridge. Ascend the upper west ridge via Class 2-3 snow and scrambling to the roomy summit. Total time from camp approximately 3-4 hours. The southwest gully is notably loose—exceptionally loose and unpleasant to climb. Descent can reverse via the gully or traverse to the lower west ridge (white-knuckle Class 3-4 scrambling with fixed sling protection at one crux).
overview: Sinister Peak is a sharp, ice-clad summit on Washington's Bulger List (the state's 100 highest peaks), rising along a high connecting ridge about 1 mile east of Dome Peak above the Chickamin and Dome Glaciers in the Glacier Peak Wilderness. It sits on the classic Ptarmigan Traverse corridor and is one of the more remote Bulgers; it was historically the final summit climbed by Russ Kroeker in October 1980 to complete the first-ever full Bulger List.

current.approach: From the Downey Creek Trailhead (elev. ~1,450') on the Suiattle River Road (FR 26), follow Downey Creek Trail #768 for 6.5 miles (easy, well-graded, mostly flat, forested trail with a suspension-bridge crossing of Downey Creek) to Sixmile Camp (2,440'), a good first-night camp with reliable water from Downey Creek. From Sixmile Camp the maintained trail ends; continue on the unmaintained Bachelor Creek climbers' path, staying on the north side of the creek initially and fording to the south side around the 9.5-mile mark (~3,700') — treat this as a real creek crossing, harder and more dangerous in high water/early season. Around 4,500' the tread largely disappears through a large avalanche-debris zone (a major slide wiped out this stretch in 2002); expect slow, brushy route-finding through slide alder and downed timber here even in good conditions, and continuous snow well below this elevation in early season. Above the debris zone the path climbs to a pass (~5,900') just northwest of Cub Lake (about 14 miles in), then drops to Cub Lake (5,338', another good camp with water). Most parties push on from Cub Lake up onto Itswoot Ridge (6,400–6,900', ~15 miles and ~5,500' of gain from the trailhead) for high camp, with sweeping views of Dome and Sinister. From high camp, traverse climbers' paths and snow benches through the upper basins (staying near 7,000') to gain the Dome Glacier, cross over the Dome–Chikamin col, and descend the Chikamin Glacier (crevassed — rope up and carry crevasse-rescue gear) to about 7,200'. Traverse right (east) across the glacier to reach the 7,640' Dome–Sinister col; a bergschrund here can be difficult to cross in late season and has occasionally required a short rappel to get down onto or across it (see descent notes — same feature is encountered both ways). From the col, contour on an easy snowfield and climb up into a loose, unpleasant gully on Sinister's south side to gain the upper west ridge, then follow a Class 2–3 scramble along the ridge to the 8,444' summit; some parties instead take the exposed Class 3+ ridge directly from the col. Loose rock in the gully is the main climbing-specific hazard on the approach to the summit block.
approach_variant_names: Downey Creek Trail #768 and the Bachelor Creek climbers' path
Two camps: the lake basin or the ridge above it
current.descent: Reverse the ascent line. Most parties downclimb the same loose south-side gully back to the Dome–Sinister col — it is one of the loosest, most unpleasant sections on the mountain, so expect care-intensive downclimbing with real rockfall risk to anyone below. A commonly preferred alternative, used by several recent parties instead of re-descending the gully, is to descend via the lower west ridge: a newer, more direct line involving sustained Class 3–4 scrambling on semi-solid rock with considerable exposure. One crux move on this ridge variant has a fixed sling left in place for protection/handline use, but this is not a rappel station — parties downclimb through it. Either way, the descent rejoins the gentle snow slopes leading back to the 7,640' Dome–Sinister col. At the col, the bergschrund that guards access to the Chikamin Glacier can be broken/unbridged in mid-to-late season; when it is, parties have used a single rappel (one 60m rope) off natural anchors (rock horn/sling or v-thread in snow, depending on conditions) to get down onto the glacier safely rather than risk a fall into the schrund — in good snow conditions or earlier in the season this same spot is often just a step-across or short downclimb with no rope work needed. From the glacier, re-ascend roughly 1,000' back to the Dome–Chikamin col, then descend to high camp on Itswoot Ridge/Cub Lake and reverse the long Bachelor Creek/Downey Creek trail back to the trailhead. Watch for loose rock in the gully, exposure on the west-ridge variant, and crevasse hazard on the Chikamin/Dome glacier crossings in both directions.
current.detailed_rack: Ice screws (4-6, 12-16 cm), snow flukes/pickets (2-3), rock nuts (half set from 0.5-2 inches), hexes (2-3), carabiners (8-10, mix of lockers and non-lockers), 50m single or 60m double rope, webbing and slings.
rack: Half set of rock nuts (0.5-2in) and 2-3 hexes
Minimal light rock rack for the summit scramble
4-6 ice screws (12-16cm) and 2-3 snow pickets/flukes for the glacier crossing
current.pro_needs: Alpine rock protection: single set of nuts and hexes (0.5-2 inches), small rack (6-8 pieces), and 50-meter rope for belay anchors on exposed ridge sections. Crampons required for glacier and snow sections.
bivy: Dome Glacier and Dome-Chickamin col high bivouacs
Bachelor Creek forest and meadow camps
current.rope_note: Class 3 with glacier crossing (Chickamin Glacier, approached via Ptarmigan Traverse). Rope up for glacier travel — crevassing and bergschrund can be serious.

name: Skeena26
beta: Pitch 1 climbs a narrow 'whale's back' of stone between facing corners on polished friction, protected by nine bolts, and holds the route's crux. Subsequent pitches ease to 5.4-5.6 with occasional 5.8 sections. The final pitch features clean splitter cracks (5.7) finishing on the buttress crest with views over Whitehorse Mountain.
overview: A 12-pitch, 1,500-ft friction climb on immaculate, knobby grey granite, with a polished 5.9 crux on pitch one easing into mostly 5.4-5.6 climbing above, finishing on clean splitter cracks overlooking Whitehorse Mountain.

current.approach: South Face is another wall within the same Squire Creek Walls complex as Waterfall Basin, reached via the same Darrington-area approach: I-5 to the Arlington exit, SR 530 east through Oso to Darrington, then Squire Creek Road to the washout-blocked parking area. From there, follow the rough, unmaintained climbers' approach — the old roadbed past a landslide crossing to a boot track that drops to a ford of Squire Creek, then a climbers' track across a tributary and up through old-growth forest into two steep, dirty gullies that top out on the grassy saddle below the South Face, roughly 3 hours from the car, with route-finding (flagging, cairns) required in several spots.
approach_variant_names: Squire Creek washout to the west saddle
current.descent: Rappel the line of ascent; 50-meter ropes are adequate for most pitches, while 60-meter ropes allow combining pitches 5 and 6 to speed the descent.
current.detailed_rack: A light single rack to 3 inches: BD Stoppers (#5-8), Black Diamond Camalot C3 (#1-2), Camalot C4 (0.5 to #3), plus 5 quickdraws and 5 alpine draws; hand-drilled stainless-steel wedge bolts protect the crux friction sections.
current.pro_needs: Bolt-protected on the polished pitch-1 crux (9 bolts) and other friction sections, with natural gear placements filling in on lower-angle pitches and the final splitter-crack pitch.
bivy: Squire Creek Park & Campground, Snohomish County
Squire Creek road end / trailhead bivouac

name: South Slopes Scramble
beta: From the Stevens Pass parking area, a route climbs past a small gray WSDOT building, under powerlines, and up a gated gravel road to Skyline Lake, then ascends northwest through timber and open slopes to a gap in the Skyline Ridge crest before following the ridge, traversing below rocky sub-points, to the summit. A faint climbers' path parallels much of the gravel-road approach and is faster than the road.
overview: Sky Mountain is the informal name for the true high point of Skyline Ridge (also called Heather Ridge on older maps), the horseshoe-shaped crest that arcs immediately north of Stevens Pass between the Tye River and Nason Creek valleys. It's the tallest summit on the ridge but is bypassed by most day-hikers, who stop at a lower, rockier sub-summit above Skyline Lake — reaching the true top requires continuing along an undulating, unofficial boot-path ridge walk. The trip is most often combined with nearby Tye Peak, which shares the same Skyline Lake approach. The summit gives views of Glacier Peak, Cowboy Mountain, Big Chief Mountain, Windy Mountain, Rock Mountain, and Lichtenberg Mountain across the Tye and Nason valleys.

current.approach: From the Stevens Pass Ski Area's north (uphill) lot, walk to the far east end of the parking area near the small gray electrical substation/WSDOT building — this is the unsigned Skyline Lake trailhead. In summer, take the gravel service road on the left side of the substation, passing beneath the powerlines; a steeper, faster boot path also splits off directly across from the WSDOT building for hikers who want to skip the road switchbacks. Follow the road/track uphill, staying left, then bear right shortly after — a vehicle gate blocks the road about a quarter mile up. The road/trail climbs steadily (roughly 500 ft of gain per half-mile in the steepest stretch) through forest and talus for about 1.2-1.3 miles to Skyline Lake (~1,100-1,300 ft gained, lake sits around 4,900-5,100 ft). Pass Skyline Lake on its south side. Just before the ground steepens into the first rocky scrambling, watch for a large boulder garden — car- to house-sized blocks — and angle southwest through/around it to regain forest on the far side; this talus-hopping section is the main route-finding wrinkle on the whole approach and is slow and ankle-twisty when wet or snow-covered. Beyond the boulder garden, gain the undulating east ridge of the horseshoe-shaped Skyline/Heather Ridge and follow it west, traversing beneath a band of rocky outcrops before the final push to Sky Mountain's summit block. Total one-way distance to the true summit is about 2.5 miles with roughly 1,400-2,600 ft of cumulative gain depending on how much of the undulating ridge is counted (the route re-gains elevation repeatedly along the ridge, which is why the recorded gain (2,600 ft) runs higher than the simple lake-to-summit elevation difference). There is no reliable water past Skyline Lake, so treat/carry water from there. The exposed south-facing slopes below the ridge are a known avalanche path — several fatal slides have occurred here in winter — so this route is best done in summer/early autumn when snow-free; a faint climbers' path is reported to persist most of the way to the summit in those conditions.
approach_variant_names: Skyline Lake and the boulder garden
current.descent: This is a walk-off, non-technical scramble descent — no rappelling. Reverse the ascent line: drop off the summit block back onto the undulating east ridge, traverse back beneath the rock outcrops, and pick your way back down through the boulder garden (take care with route-finding here in fog or late in the day, since the talus field has no single obvious line). From the boulder garden, regain the trail/road past Skyline Lake's south shore and descend the service road/boot path back to the Stevens Pass ski area north lot. Stay alert on the ridge and the open south-facing slopes for wind-loaded snow or wet, loose rock; the ridge's minor ups and downs mean the descent regains and loses elevation a few times rather than being a straight shot down.
current.rope_note: Class 2 scramble; described as non-technical, requiring more time/navigation than nearby peaks due to steep approach slopes, but no rope or technical gear needed.

name: Slippery Slab Tower NE Face
beta: This is a two-pitch alpine rock climb that functions as a half-day objective after the long approach. Pitch 1 involves a low 5th class move followed by class 3 scrambling to a large tree belay (40 feet). Pitch 2 features face climbing transitioning to a gully, then exposed slab to the summit (50+ feet). The route can be climbed as one full 60m pitch or broken into two for better communication. A climbing register is present at the summit. Despite its name, this route is neither slippery nor a slab.
overview: A short, moderate two-pitch rock climb up the northeast arete/shoulder of Slippery Slab Tower, a slender granite pinnacle near Thunder Mountain above Trap Pass, ending at a summit register after a long, scenic wilderness approach.

current.approach: From either trailhead, climbers first gain the Pacific Crest Trail — via the Tunnel Creek Trail climbing about 1,170 ft in 1.45 miles to Hope Lake, or via the Surprise Creek Trail to Surprise Lake — then follow the PCT to Trap Pass (~5,800 ft), south from Hope Lake or north from the Surprise Lake side. From Trap Pass an unmaintained climbers' trail continues south along the ridge to the base of Slippery Slab Tower, with Thunder Mountain further along the same ridgeline above Glacier Lake. The round trip is long enough (roughly 6 miles one-way) that many parties camp overnight at Hope Lake or Trap Lake.
approach_variant_names: Tunnel Creek trail to the crest trail at the lake, then south to the pass
Surprise Creek trail past the two lakes, then the switchbacks to the pass
current.descent: From the summit, make two rappels down the climbing route to return to the base of the tower. Climbers typically use a 60m rope doubled for each rappel, or make multiple 30-50m single-strand rappels. Be mindful of loose, pointy rocks during the descent. Once back at the base, scramble back through the pass terrain to Trap Pass, then reverse the PCT and Tunnel Creek Trail descent.
current.detailed_rack: Nuts and light rack of small to medium cams (BD#0.4-#2). Include a .3-3 size range of nuts. Bring slings and extra webbing for anchor building. Rap rings and extra cordage recommended for backup rappel anchors.
current.pro_needs: Protection is readily available on this route with good placements in cracks and corners. Nuts and small to medium cams are the primary protection. Slings around natural features (trees, horns) provide secure anchors.
current.rope_note: 2-pitch 5.4 route from the NE shoulder: P1 is a short low-5th move up/right to scrubby trees, P2 continues to the ridge. Descent is by rappelling the route from belay trees.

name: Corkscrew Route
beta: From either the Bedal Creek or Cougar Creek (North Fork Sauk) trailhead, a climber's trail leaves the maintained tread and climbs through forest and talus to a saddle near Bedal Peak, then crosses the Sloan Glacier. Parties step off the glacier at the Southeast ridge and follow a boot path that corkscrews south then north around the South ridge, finishing with a short, exposed 3rd/4th-class scramble to the summit.
overview: The classic ascent of Sloan Peak's distinctive horn. The route literally spirals around the mountain, crossing the Sloan Glacier and finishing with an exposed Class 3 scramble to the summit. A Mountain Loop landmark visible for miles.

current.approach: Most parties start from the Bedal Creek trailhead at about 2,800 ft, at the end of a rough high-clearance spur (Forest Road 4096) off the Mountain Loop Highway a mile or so past the Bedal campground. Follow the Bedal Creek trail through old-growth forest and along the creek to where a large washout has taken the tread; scramble the washout to a cairned exit, then climb the climbers' path through forest and onto talus and meadow to the saddle near 5,300 ft, the last dependable water. From there bear toward the moraine and the lower glacier. A second, less used approach starts from the pullout on Sloan Creek Road and fords the North Fork Sauk River, then follows Cougar Creek; it avoids the Bedal road, but the crossings are dangerous in high water, mainly May through July.
approach_variant_names: Bedal Creek Trail #705 (FR 4096)
North Fork Sauk / Cougar Creek (FR 49)
current.descent: Descent reverses the ascent line: from the summit, downclimb the short, low-5th-class/exposed Class 4 step about 100 ft below the true summit (the 'bear hug' move on the ridge has solid hand cracks on both sides and is usually downclimbed free by competent parties). Parties uncomfortable downclimbing it can rig a short hand line or single-strand rappel here — there is no fixed/bolted anchor; build off a rock horn, chockstone, or gear placement, and a single 30 m/60 m rope doubled is more than enough for the ~15-20 ft of steep rock involved. Below that, follow cairns and the climbers' trail back along the south-face heather ledges and the loose scree/dirt gully that gained access from the ledge system — this gully is notably loose underfoot and the ledges above it have real exposure (parties have noted a ~500 ft unprotected drop at the outer edge), so downclimb it carefully rather than glissading or rushing. At the base of the gully/ledges, re-rope for the glacier crossing back to the toe where gear was staged, then continue down slabs to the basin/saddle. From there it's a full reversal of whichever approach was used — steep scree/slab and forest switchbacks back to the Cougar Creek waterfall and North Fork Sauk crossings (Sloan Creek/FR 49 approach), or the Bedal Creek climbers' path and old trail (Bedal Creek/FS 4096 approach) — down to the trailhead. This is a walk-off/downclimb descent with no standard rappelling on the glacier or ledges; the only rope use besides glacier travel is the optional short hand line/rappel off the summit step described above. Total car-to-car time for strong parties runs roughly 9-13 hours depending on approach and conditions; snow lingering on the basin/ledges into early summer, and afternoon softening of the glacier snowpack on hot days, are the main descent-timing hazards.
current.detailed_rack: Glacier kit; rope for glacier and short summit-block belay; light rack optional for summit pitch.
current.pro_needs: Minimal rock pro; mainly glacier protection.

name: Standard Route (Southwest Slopes)
beta: From the Snow Lake trailhead at Alpental, find an unsigned boot path just off an old dirt road. The path climbs a steep, loose creek bed through forest for about a mile to a junction (right forks to Guye Peak/Cave Ridge; stay left/straight for the summit). Continue past a roughly 50-ft waterfall to an open meadow between Snoqualmie Mountain and Cave Ridge, then switchback up open southwest-facing slopes to the summit. Most parties treat it as a there-and-back half-day trip; it is popular as both a snow-free scramble and, with an ice axe/crampons, a winter/spring snow climb.
overview: Snoqualmie Mountain is the highest summit rising directly above the Alpental ski area at Snoqualmie Pass, one of the most-climbed scrambles near Seattle for its short approach and big views of Chair Peak, The Tooth, and Guye Peak across the valley. The peak actually has two summits about 550 ft apart: the popular west summit reached by this standard climbers' path, and a slightly higher east summit (about 3 ft taller per a 2023 professional GPS survey). The direct ridge between them involves an exposed 5th-class downclimb; the easier way drops around the south side of the summit block and gains the east summit by an exposed 3rd-class east ridge — most parties doing the standard route skip it.

current.approach: Park in the Alpental lot at the end of Alpental Rd (NW Forest Pass required at the trailhead kiosk). Walk toward the signed Snow Lake trailhead, but instead of taking that trail, look for an unsigned boot path/old roadbed about 50 ft downhill (south) of the Snow Lake trailhead sign, dropping into a band of slide alder — this is the shared start for both Guye Peak and Snoqualmie Mountain. The path immediately steepens and follows a creek drainage (Source Creek) up through roots, talus, and brush; it is a climbers' path only, not a maintained trail, and can be hard to follow in the alder in early season or after blowdown. At roughly 1 mile / ~1,000 ft gain, a junction splits: the right fork climbs to Guye Peak and Cave Ridge proper, while the main Snoqualmie route continues left/straight. About a third of a mile past that junction the path fords the creek near a 50-ft waterfall (the main water source on route — treat before drinking); a quarter mile beyond the crossing it breaks out of the trees onto the open west-facing gully/slope below Cave Ridge and switchbacks steeply up this slope for roughly the final mile to the summit ridge and the true summit at 6,278 ft. Expect loose scree and dirt underfoot throughout, exposure on the last stretch of ridge before the top, and lingering snow in the gully well into summer — an ice axe and traction are commonly carried into June. Total is about 3.8 miles round trip with 3,100+ ft of gain, though it is sometimes given as closer to 5 miles depending on exactly where mileage is measured from.
approach_variant_names: The unsigned boot path 50 ft below the Snow Lake trailhead sign
current.descent: This is a walk-off, not a rappel route — descend by reversing the ascent gully/climbers' path back down through Cave Ridge's west slope, past the waterfall creek crossing and the Guye Peak junction, to the Alpental lot. No rappelling or fixed anchors are involved (rappels = 0). The descent is the crux for many parties: the scree/dirt path is looser and harder to control on the way down than it looks going up, and the upper gully holds snow into summer, so in spring conditions a glissade down the snow-filled chute is a common (faster) alternative to the dry boot path — carry an ice axe and know self-arrest if attempting it, since the gully funnels into trees and rock lower down. In winter and spring this same gully is recognized avalanche terrain (a frequent subject of NWAC-relevant trip reports and Mountaineers winter scramble/ski trip logs), so check avalanche conditions and be prepared to bail to Cave Ridge rather than push through unstable snow. Watch footing carefully near the top where the ridge narrows and exposure increases just below the summit.
current.pro_needs: None in dry summer conditions.
current.rope_note: Class 2-3 scramble via SW slopes/Cave Ridge; roped travel not standard. Some parties carry a 20-30m handline + prusik for a short exposed step near the summit ridge. Helmet strongly recommended for climber-induced rockfall in the talus field.

name: Neve Glacier / Standard Route
beta: From the Pyramid Lake Trailhead, hike the well-worn trail to Pyramid Lake (~2 mi), then follow a steep, less-traveled climbers' trail up the East Ridge of Pyramid Peak into alpine terrain. Traverse south past the east flank of Paul Bunyan's Stump onto the Colonial Glacier, climb ~30-degree snow to the Colonial-Neve col (~6,800-6,840 ft), then descend roughly 150-250 ft onto the Neve Glacier. Rope up and cross the Neve — parties describe the cleanest line through the center of its crevasse field — to the ridge near The Horseman on Snowfield's west side (~7,700 ft), then finish with roughly 400-600 ft of class 3-4 (occasionally class 5 on variant lines) rock scrambling to the summit.
overview: Snowfield Peak (8,351 ft) is the high point of the Colonial/Neve group in the North Cascades National Park core, about 5 miles ESE of Newhalem. Its defining feature is the roughly 750-acre Neve Glacier draping its north and northwest flanks — one of the larger non-volcanic glaciers in the Washington Cascades — crossed en route to an easy but exposed class 3-4 scramble to the summit.

current.approach: From the Pyramid Lake Trailhead (~1,150-1,200 ft, a signed gravel pullout on the north side of SR-20 near milepost 126.8, about 21 miles east of Marblemount just past the Diablo turnoff), follow the well-maintained Pyramid Lake Trail as it climbs steadily through old-growth forest. A rock-hop creek crossing at roughly 1 mile is the last easy, reliable water before the lake. At 2.1 miles and about 1,500 ft of gain you reach Pyramid Lake (~2,600 ft) - top off water here, since the next several hours offer little. From the lake's south/right side, pick up the unmaintained but well-trodden climbers' path; it is steep and brushy from the outset and gains roughly 2,000 ft more, switchbacking up to the East Ridge of Pyramid Peak (~4,000 ft), then follows the narrow, knolly ridge crest past Point 4,555 ft toward Pyramid Peak, with loose rock and short routefinding steps. Just short of Pyramid Peak, descend slightly and traverse - often on lingering snow - across scree and boulders to the terminal moraine and small lake at the base of the Colonial Glacier (~5,900-6,100 ft), the standard first camp, with a tarn for water. From camp, rope up for glacier travel (crevasses present) and climb the Colonial Glacier south to the broad Colonial-Neve col (~6,800-6,900 ft; a stream/waterfall here is a second good camp and water source), then descend about 200 ft onto the Neve Glacier and cross it - a moderate, usually well-tracked but crevassed glacier crossing requiring a rope - to the rocks just below Snowfield's summit pyramid on its northwest side. From there a long class 3 gully leads to a notch below the true summit; the final short traverse/scramble across the notch to the south side and up to the summit (8,351 ft) is exposed class 3, with one move occasionally rated low class 4. Given roughly 7,300 ft of total gain and sustained glacier travel, most parties treat this as a 2-day (overnight) objective rather than a single push.
approach_variant_names: Pyramid Lake trail and the Pyramid Peak east ridge to the Colonial Glacier moraine camp
Carrying through to the col camp above the Colonial Glacier
current.descent: Descent reverses the ascent line rather than following an independent route. From the summit, downclimb the exposed class 3 (occasionally low class 4) notch and gully back down to the rocks above the Neve Glacier, then retrace the glacier crossing - roped, watching for crevasses and softening snow bridges later in the day - back up to the Colonial-Neve col. From the col, descend the Colonial Glacier (many parties glissade its moderate snow slopes where safe, keeping clear of its crevasses) back to the moraine-lake camp, then reverse the climbers' path and ridge crest over Point 4,555 ft down to Pyramid Lake, finishing on the maintained Pyramid Lake Trail back to the trailhead. In standard summer conditions this is a walk-off/downclimb with no rappelling required - the summit notch is a class 3 downclimb reversed on the way out. In early-season, icy, or thin-snow conditions, however, parties have rappelled the notch instead of downclimbing it: one winter party describes building a two-picket snow anchor and making a single-strand rappel with a 30m rope (noting 30m was plenty of length for that pitch), then prusiking back up the same line on their return ascent. Treat that rappel as conditions-dependent rather than a fixed feature of the route - there are no bolted or fixed anchors anywhere on this route, so a party that might need it should carry a picket or two and a single 30m-or-longer rope as a contingency. Primary descent hazards are crevasse fall on both the Colonial and Neve glaciers (rope up and probe softening snow bridges, especially in the afternoon), loose rock on the ridge and gully sections, and North Cascades whiteout/navigation risk - the Pyramid Peak ridge and glacier crossings have few visual reference points in cloud, so many parties track their ascent line with GPS for the return.
current.detailed_rack: Pickets and slings for the glacier, plus a few small pieces for the short Class 4 summit rock.
current.pro_needs: Roped glacier travel on the Neve Glacier, then a short exposed Class 4 scramble to the summit block; minimal rock pro needed.

name: Standard Route / Snowking Glacier
beta: This is the most-used of Snowking's standard lines and the one essentially every documented party takes, chosen for its directness, though it starts low (about 2,300 ft) and doesn't tour the whole mountain. Most groups treat it as a two-day trip with a bivy near Cyclone Lake, though strong parties have done it car-to-car in a long day (9-14 hrs) on firm spring snow. It is glacier travel, not technical climbing — ice axe, crampons, and a rope with basic crevasse-rescue gear are standard, and parties are advised to stay roped through the upper snowfield/glacier, especially once blue ice and crevasses open up in high summer.
overview: Snowking Mountain is a remote, heavily glaciated high point in the Mount Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, about 18 miles northeast of Darrington and roughly 10 miles southwest of Cascade Pass. Its summit massif spans more than 10 square miles with two subsidiary summits (West Peak, ~7,425 ft; Middle Peak, ~7,400 ft) and the unnamed 'Snowking Glacier' on its north face. Long, brushy, largely unmaintained approaches off the Cascade River Road keep it lightly visited relative to its size and prominence.

current.approach: Drive Cascade River Road ~14.2 miles from Marblemount and turn right onto FR-1570 (Kindy Creek Road). The road crosses the Cascade River on a concrete bridge; within roughly 0.4 mile the right fork is blocked by boulders/washout and parking is at that Y-junction (around 1,160-1,200ft). From here the true 'approach' begins as a road-walk: follow the closed roadbed (windfall, brush encroachment, washouts that keep it permanently closed to vehicles) for about 2-3 miles, gaining roughly 1,000ft, to a small clearing/end-of-road firepit near 2,300ft. Watch on the left for a steep, easy-to-miss climbers' path leaving the old roadbed into the trees - this is unsigned and has no official trail number. The path climbs steeply through brush and then old-growth forest on a boot-beaten tread over roots and rock, with no reliable water until well upslope, so top off at the last Cascade River-side crossing if possible. Around 4,800ft there's a boggy bench with a tent spot (first realistic camp/rest option and an intermittent water source). Near 5,200ft the path forks at a signed-by-cairn junction where a fainter 'fisherman's trail' drops toward Found Lake; stay right/uphill on the climbers' path, which steepens over Point 5,791 and follows the Kindy Ridge crest past Found Peak (~5,400ft) and Point 5,695. The ridge undulates - expect several short ups and downs rather than continuous gain - before dropping slightly to the meadows and tarn on the east side of Cyclone Lake (roughly 5,500-6,200ft), the standard high camp with reliable water and the best campsites on the route. From camp, traverse below or over Peak 5,860 heading toward Snowking's east side, then gain the Snowking Glacier proper. In late season this is a straightforward snow/heather slope (~1,900ft over about 1.3 miles to the summit), but by mid-to-late summer the glacier opens up with exposed blue ice and real crevasses - rope up for glacier travel and carry basic crevasse-rescue gear rather than treating it as a snow plod. Most parties treat this as a two-day trip (car to Cyclone Lake camp, then summit day), though strong parties in good conditions do it car-to-car in 12-14 hours.
approach_variant_names: The closed Kindy Creek roadbed and the Kindy Ridge climbers' path to the lake meadows
Two camps: the lake meadows or the benches above them
current.descent: Descend the same way you came up: reverse the Snowking Glacier/east-ridge line back toward Cyclone Lake. This is a walk-off, not a rappelling route - no fixed anchors or rappels are typically needed on the standard line, so plan on downclimbing and glacier travel rather than roped lowers. The main hazard is timing: by afternoon, sun-softened, sun-cupped snow bridges over the glacier's crevasses become unreliable, so descend the icy/crevassed upper section earlier in the day if possible and keep the rope team spread out and probing rather than following a single boot track blindly. Below the glacier, pick your way back over/around Peak 5,860 to the Cyclone Lake meadows (camp), then reverse the Kindy Ridge undulations over Point 5,791, Found Peak, and Point 5,695, staying right at the 5,200ft junction to avoid dropping toward Found Lake on the fisherman's trail. From the 4,800ft boggy bench, follow the boot path back down through old growth and brush to the old FR-1570 roadbed, then road-walk the final 2-3 miles out to the car at the washout/gate. Loose duff, roots, and brush on the steep upper boot path are the main footing hazards on the way down; there is no technical rock descent or established rappel sequence on this route.
current.detailed_rack: Pickets and slings for the glacier; minimal rock gear needed.
current.pro_needs: Standard glacier-travel kit — rope, a few pickets or ice screws, and crevasse-rescue gear; no rock protection is needed for the Class 2-3 summit scramble.
bivy: Cyclone Lake and the lakes just north of it
Found Lake and the Kindy Ridge saddle

name: Direct East Buttress
beta: Ascend the prominent East Buttress via mixed rock and bolt-ladder terrain. Route is largely 5.8-5.9 with two crux pitches of 5.11 and one 5.10 connector. Bolt ladders on pitches 4 and 6 allow grade flexibility; many parties now free-climb the route entirely at 5.11.
overview: The direct version of South Early Winter Spire's classic East Buttress, climbing harder, steeper pitches low on the buttress before joining the upper line. A sustained, high-quality alpine rock route on excellent Washington Pass granite.

current.approach: Park at the 'hairpin' pullout on Highway 20 (separate from the Blue Lake Trailhead), hike up Spire Gully following occasional cairns to the last large tree in the gully, then traverse right across talus (or snow early-season — bring crampons/axe) to the gully leading to the notch between North and South Early Winters Spire, then traverse left to the base of the east buttress. Roughly 1.5 hours car-to-base at a moderate pace; the line is visible from the road.
approach_variant_names: Spire Gully from the SR-20 hairpin (dry)
Early-season, snow in Spire Gully
current.descent: Downclimb the South Arete from the summit — mostly 3rd/4th class with one short, more exposed 5th-class section — down to bolted anchors above the standard SEWS descent gully, then make 3 single-rope rappels (60m rope) from bolted anchors/chains to the base of the wall. From the base, hike out via the climber's trail to the Blue Lake Trail; if you parked at the hairpin rather than the Blue Lake Trailhead, plan a short road walk or car shuttle back.
current.detailed_rack: Double rack of small to medium cams, a set of nuts, and extra small pieces for the thin crux pitches.
current.pro_needs: Emphasis on small-to-medium protection for the sustained, harder direct pitches.

name: South Face
beta: Two-pitch technical rock climb on solid granite. The South Face receives consistent sun, making it a good choice early and late in the season. Approach via Burgundy Col from Highway 20. Descent via North Ridge scramble or rappel.
overview: A friendly two-pitch alpine rock route on solid granite offering excellent views and moderate technical climbing with good protection opportunities.

current.approach: From the pullout, find a faint boot path descending loose talus/scree to the east into the trees, passing a trail register, then crossing Early Winters Creek on a log (~4,080 ft). The trail climbs the timbered rib north of Burgundy Creek, steeply gaining elevation to a basin/camp bench around 6,500 ft (roughly 2 hours from the car), then continues up to Burgundy Col (~7,800 ft, ~3 hours). Vasiliki Tower rises directly from the north side of the col; good camping and a late-season spring are near 6,400-6,500 ft.
approach_variant_names: Burgundy Creek rib to Burgundy Col
current.descent: From the summit, climbers typically descend via the North Ridge, a fun and easy Class 3 scramble back to Burgundy Col. The North Ridge descent takes approximately 1 hour round trip from summit to col. Alternatively, rappel stations may be used for a faster descent.
current.detailed_rack: Bring selection of nuts, cams (0.5 to 3 size range), and slings. Granite offers good protection opportunities. A single 60m rope suffices, reaching the stations with a little easy downclimbing between them, and a 70m rope reaches each station outright; two 30m ropes joined give the same 30 m rappel as a doubled 60m.
rack: Two 30m ropes for rappel, or single 60m dry rope
current.pro_needs: The South Face offers numerous cracks for traditional protection. Good natural anchors at belay stations. Moderate climbing with good protection throughout.
bivy: Bench Camp — larch bench above the Wine Spires pullout
current.rope_note: Nuts, cams from about 0.5 to 3, and slings - the granite takes natural gear well and the belays are good natural anchors. The rappel stations are in place, and what decides your rope is reach between them: a 70 m gets from one station to the next, a 60 m just does it with a little easy downclimbing in between, and two 30 m ropes joined give the same 30 m rappel as a doubled 60. Many parties skip the rappels altogether and scramble the Class 3 North Ridge back to Burgundy Col, which is about an hour round trip from the summit.

name: South Face
beta: Follows the obvious weakness — the only reasonable passage — up the south face toward the bunny-ear notch on good cracks with solid protection, through a right-facing corner, finishing on a splitter thin-hands pitch on excellent granite before an A0 aid move off a bolt to reach the summit.
overview: The South Face is Pernod Spire's other established rock line, right of the 1952 Standard Route, first climbed by Peter Jewitt, Cliff Leight, and Dan Waters on July 10, 1988. It is rated 5.9 (HVS 5a) with a short A0 aid section on the original line.

current.approach: From the SR-20 pullout near milepost 166 (0.7 mile past the Cutthroat Lake Road turnoff), the climbers' trail drops off the highway, crosses Early Winters Creek almost immediately (around 4,080 ft, via logs), and climbs steeply — gaining nearly 2,400 ft — to the bench camp at roughly 6,460-6,500 ft, the standard staging area for all the Wine Spires. From there the trail works up scree gullies to 7,770-ft Burgundy Col. Rather than dropping straight to Pernod's south side from the col, most parties continue traversing/scrambling around the east (Silver Star Creek) side of the ridge below Chianti, aiming for the notch between Pernod and Chablis — expect loose 4th-class terrain on this stretch. Because the South Face is short (Grade II, 2 pitches, 5.9) and sits tucked between Pernod's bigger west face and Chablis, many parties approach it as a linkup: climb Chablis' East Face first, then downclimb or make a short rappel across loose rock to reach the base of Pernod's south face rather than committing to the full traverse from Burgundy Col. Either way, carry a rope for the final approach moves and expect loose rock underfoot the whole way in.
approach_variant_names: Burgundy Col, then the loose fourth-class traverse round the east side below Chianti to the Pernod-Chablis notch
current.descent: This is not a walk-off — the way down is by rappel. From the summit area, one commonly used anchor is a two-piton station equalized with cord; the short aid block just below the top is protected by a mix of one newer bolt and one old quarter-inch bolt with an aging hanger — treat the old bolt with real suspicion. Rappel the south face to the Pernod-Chablis notch on two ropes (60m ropes recommended; a single 70m can just barely work, but a 60m single can leave you several meters short of the notch). Watch for rope-eating cracks a few feet below a slung-horn rap station — build that anchor as high as practical so the rope doesn't jam on the pull. From the notch, a short 4th-class scramble regains the East Face rappel line on Chablis, and two double-rope rappels down that line reach the base, rather than re-climbing back over to Burgundy Col. If you're descending independently instead of via Chablis, reverse the traverse below Chianti back to Burgundy Col and follow the climbers' path down the scree gullies to the bench camp and boot path to the highway.
current.detailed_rack: A moderate trad rack: 2x 0.3-2" BD Camalots, one set of stoppers, a 0.2" BD cam, and #3/#4 Camalots recommended for the wider cracks; about 10 alpine draws and two 60m ropes.
current.pro_needs: Good, solid crack protection throughout; the final summit move is A0 off a fixed bolt rather than free climbable at the stated grade.
bivy: Burgundy Col high camp — west side, the Wine Spires
Burgundy Creek bench camp — west side
Upper scree benches below Burgundy Col — west side
current.rope_note: 5.9 with one A0 aid move; standard trad rack sufficient, optional aider/daisy for the A0 section.

name: South Face
beta: The easiest of Concord's standard routes. Start with a class-2 walk across gravelly, gently down-sloping ledges to the first belay, then climb up and right toward trees. A roped scramble along the ridge crest leads to a sandy stance near a feature climbers call the 'shark fin.' The final pitch climbs up and over the shark fin and onto the summit block, belaying from bolts at the top. Rock quality and protection are good throughout.
overview: A sunnier, less-trafficked alternative to Concord's classic North Face, the South Face climbs broken corners and cracks up the peak's south side to the same small, exposed summit block. It's commonly linked with Lexington Tower's North Face or Liberty Bell's Beckey Route via the shared notch for an efficient multi-tower day.

current.approach: Drive Highway 20 (North Cascades Highway) to the Blue Lake Trailhead (~5,400 ft), on the south side of the highway about 30 miles west of Winthrop and roughly 1 mile west of the Washington Pass Overlook; pay the day-use fee or display a Northwest Forest/Interagency pass (the ~20-car lot fills early). Hike the Blue Lake Trail about 1.5 miles to a small meadow, then leave the trail on a climber's boot path that breaks off just past a small stream. Follow this path up through slabs, talus, and heather to the base of the gully between Concord and Lexington Towers, then climb that gully (often snow- or ice-filled into late June) to the Concord-Lexington notch. The South Face routes are reached from the notch or by working around the tower's east/south side from there.
approach_variant_names: Blue Lake Trail to the Concord-Lexington notch
current.descent: Downclimb or make one full double-rope rappel from the summit back to the notch; with a single rope, use two shorter rappels off intermediate anchor stations partway down the south face instead.
current.detailed_rack: A single rack of cams from 0.4 to 3 inches plus a set of stoppers and several double-length slings covers the wandering corners and cracks; two 60m ropes allow the full-length rappel from the summit back to the notch in one, and a party carrying a single rope makes two shorter rappels off the intermediate anchor stations partway down the south face instead.
current.pro_needs: Modest rack; mostly moderate corners and cracks with occasional wandering protection.

name: South Face
beta: A long, alpine-feeling line with sections where rock quality and protection vary considerably; route-finding is non-trivial and some sections carry real fall consequences. Far less traveled than the North or Northwest Faces.
overview: A seven-pitch, III 5.8 line up Kangaroo Temple's South Face — the longest and most sustained of the peak's moderate routes, with variable rock quality and genuine route-finding challenge.

current.approach: The Temple (Kangaroo Temple, on Kangaroo Ridge) is reached from the large pullout at the hairpin turns on SR-20 just east of Washington Pass — the same parking area used for the neighboring Hairpin Crags/Spire Gully climbs. From the pullout, a climber's trail heads south across a boulder field, through forest and more talus (faint, intermittently cairned) up to Kangaroo Pass, about 1 hour. From the pass, an intermittent trail traverses to a gully between Kangaroo Temple and Little Finger; ascending or descending that gully reaches the base of the North Face, Northwest Face, or Southwest Face routes, roughly another hour. Important — this route shares the approach to Kangaroo Pass with Temple's North/Northwest Face routes but finishes differently: rather than climbing toward the notch, drop some elevation below the pass and traverse across to the base of the South Face, roughly 2-4 hours from the car in all. The face isn't visible from the highway.
approach_variant_names: The Hairpin turnout and Kangaroo Pass, then drop below the pass and traverse to the South Face
current.descent: Descend by rappel down the North Face; nothing is left at the base of the South Face, so carry everything over the top. From the summit, scramble with some exposure out to the rappel anchor above the north face — it is not obvious and cannot be seen until you are a few feet from it. Two double-rope rappels, or three with a single 60 m rope, reach the notch between the Temple and Little Finger. Descend the loose gully below the notch, traverse back to Kangaroo Pass, and follow the climbers' trail down to the hairpin.
current.detailed_rack: Double set of cams from 0.4-3", a single #4 cam (optional #5), and a full set of nuts/stoppers. Rock quality and protection vary through the route, with some sections sparsely protected.
current.pro_needs: Double cams (0.4-3"), one #4 cam (optional #5), and nuts. Route-finding and inconsistent rock quality mean some placements will be marginal — this is a more serious route than a bare 5.8 rating implies.
bivy: SR 20 climbers' pullouts — the hairpin and the Silver Star Creek pullout
Lone Fir, Klipchuck and Early Winters campgrounds
current.rope_note: 7-pitch III 5.8 route up slabs/cracks/chimneys (also referenced as Southwest Face). Descent via hidden 3-bolt anchors (no chains) atop the North Face and at the P1 belay, 3 single-rope raps with a 60m rope.

name: South Face Center
beta: Follows the obvious crack in the middle of the south face wall starting from the notch: climb through a bulge, then trend left through two right-facing corners to a tree just below the summit block. At 220 feet, the whole route goes in one pitch with a 70m rope (or can be broken into two with a 60m rope). The route wanders, so expect to place extra alpine draws to manage rope drag; some loose blocks and flakes are present and the rock carries lichen from relatively light traffic.
overview: A shorter, steeper variation up the center of Concord's south face, starting about 100 ft climber's-left (west) of the standard South Face line. It climbs the center crack through a bulge and two right-facing corners to a tree just below the summit block, then on to the top.

current.approach:
Drive Highway 20 to the Blue Lake Trailhead (~5,400 ft), about 30 miles west of Winthrop and about a mile west of the Washington Pass Overlook; a day-use fee or Northwest Forest/Interagency pass is required and the small lot fills early. Hike the Blue Lake Trail about 1.5 miles until it opens out, then take the well-established climbers' path on the left, marked by a large cairn.

The South Face routes are reached from the Concord-Lexington notch, which is a different saddle from the Liberty Bell-Concord col that the North Face and the Beckey Route use. Rather than trending toward the Liberty Bell-Concord gully, keep working up and left into the gully between Concord and Lexington Towers; higher up, a reasonable climbers' path appears along its left side and is better than fighting up the gully bed. It sees far less traffic than the Liberty Bell-Concord col.

You are at the right saddle when Concord is on one side of you and Lexington on the other, and the Concord wall in front of you gives onto low-angle, gravelly ledges rather than a steep crack system. If you are facing a crack system, you are at the Liberty Bell-Concord notch and looking at the North Face.

There is no approach detail specific to South Face Center beyond this shared approach.
approach_variant_names: Blue Lake Trail, then up and left into the Concord-Lexington gully rather than the Liberty Bell-Concord one
current.descent: Downclimb or make one full double-rope rappel from the summit back to the notch; with a single rope, use two shorter rappels off intermediate anchor stations instead.
current.detailed_rack: A rack to about #3 (roughly 1.5 sets), plus extra alpine draws given how much the route wanders; a bolted anchor awaits at the top.
rack: Stoppers, plus small cams/RPs for thin sections
Single dynamic rope (a 70m rope lets you climb it as one pitch)
current.pro_needs: Gear up to #3 with about 1.5 sets covers the route; because it wanders through the bulge and corners, bring extra slings/draws to control rope drag.
current.rope_note: Verified: climbable in one ~220ft (67m) pitch with a 70m rope; two single-rope rappels from the south side of the summit for descent. Loose blocks/flakes — usual alpine caution.

name: South Face
beta: From Edward Mesa (the 'Lost World Plateau'), descend to the south side of the peak to a steep gully marked by a giant chockstone. Pitch 1 climbs 15 feet of 5.7 to a tree; subsequent pitches traverse ledges, include a chimney with a 5.6 downclimb, a 5.7 flake with stemming, and scrambling through boulders and trees to the top.
overview: The original 1948 first-ascent line up The Mole (Edward Peak) — a 4-pitch, Grade II moderate alpine rock route up the peak's south side, reached via a steep gully with a distinctive giant chockstone.

current.approach: Two main approach options: via the Snow Creek trail (leaving it around 3,200 ft) or via the Hook Creek drainage from Icicle Creek Lane. Both lead up to Edward Mesa (the 'Lost World Plateau'), from which climbers descend to the south side of Edward Peak to a steep gully holding a giant chockstone.
current.descent: Descend either by rappelling off natural anchors (a boulder with slings/bolt, or a horn rappel station) or by downclimbing the ascent line.
current.detailed_rack: Gear to 3 inches.
current.pro_needs: Standard rack to 3 inches covers the route's cracks and flakes.

name: South Gully/South Spur
beta: Crux is negotiating one or two chockstones jammed in the gully -- parties are typically forced left onto the adjacent face (or stem/squeeze past on sometimes wet, loose rock) before regaining the gully and following the South Spur to the top. Protection is sparse and low-5th-class: a small rack of cams and nuts plus slung trees, with a hand line sometimes rigged over the exposed ground above the chockstones.
overview: Alpine gully route up Guye Peak's south side: climbs a chockstone-choked gully, then exits onto the South Spur for the final push to the summit. Popular moderate objective near Snoqualmie Pass, climbed as a summer/fall scramble and, under snow, in winter.

current.approach: From I-90 Exit 52, follow Alpental Road up to the ski area and park at the Alpental ski-area lot (the Snow Lake trailhead parking) or in a legal spot along Alpental Road itself. The side roads named 'Strasse' are private, and since 2021 residents have barred climbers from driving or walking on them. For the south-face/rock routes, the crag rises directly above the parking area with essentially no approach hike required. For routes on other aspects of the mountain, use the Commonwealth Basin/PCT North Trailhead a short distance up the highway instead, following the Pacific Crest Trail into Commonwealth Basin before cutting up toward the peak. Because of the short, direct access, Guye Peak is climbed both summer and winter, though rock routes are primarily a snow-free-season (summer-fall) objective.
approach_variant_names: Winter and spring: Commonwealth Basin from Summit West, straight at the gully
Summer and autumn: the south side of the peak from Alpental, as a dry scramble
current.descent: From the south summit, traverse the connecting ridge to Guye's middle summit, then make a roughly 30-meter rappel from slung trees down to the north summit. From there, descend west via the Cave Ridge climbers' trail back toward Alpental, or alternatively east via the Commonwealth Basin trail — this is the shared standard descent for Guye Peak's south-side lines.
current.detailed_rack: A 60m rope for handline sections and the summit rappel; a light rack of small-to-medium nuts and cams up to about a #2 Camalot covers the chockstone/crux exit, with 2-3 slings for tree or rock rappel anchors. Conditions-dependent — some parties report needing little beyond the chockstone move.
current.pro_needs: A small rock rack, a single rope, and slings for trees; many parties simul-climb or solo the easier gully sections rather than pitching the whole route out.
current.rope_note: Guye Peak, Easy 5th class/Grade II. Small rock rack, single rope, slings for tree anchors.

name: South Headwall
beta: 5.8 YDS / VI- UIAA Grade II Alpine. 5 pitches trad climbing with 4–5 technical pitches. Two 20–30 ft sections of 5.7; extensive 4th–5th class scrambling. Hazards: frequent rockfall, loose rock/choss, exposure, early-season snow/ice. Requires cams, stoppers, long slings. Best June–August (peak July); avoid late season. First Ascent: Myhre & Sorenson (1966).
overview: A moderate 4-5 pitch rock route up the steep (but not vertical) headwall visible just below the summit on the south side, topping out very near the true summit.

current.approach: Northeast via Ingalls Way Trail #1390 and Longs Pass Trail #1229, then down to Ingalls Creek; ascend first major clearing west of Ulrich's Couloir
approach_variant_names: Longs Pass to Ingalls Creek, then the first major clearing west of Ulrich's Couloir
current.descent: The route tops out very close to the true summit, so the way down is the Cascadian Couloir to the south. Cross the Class 2-3 ground between the true and false summits (steep, often corniced snow early in the season), then drop into the couloir and follow it down loose scree and talus to Ingalls Creek. The headwall base lies up-basin along the same drainage, so collect anything left there, then climb back to Longs Pass and walk out to the Esmeralda trailhead. Carry an ice axe through at least midsummer, and stay out from under other parties, as the couloir is notoriously loose.
current.detailed_rack: Cams and stoppers for mostly 4th/low-5th terrain plus two short 5.7 sections; long slings for wandering belays. No fixed gear reported.
current.pro_needs: A standard rack of cams and nuts is sufficient; ledges provide belay stations for every pitch.
bivy: Ingalls Creek basin camp, below Longs Pass
current.rope_note: 4-5 short technical pitches (mostly 4th/low-5th) with two 20-30 ft sections of 5.7 that have decent pro; approach via Ingalls Creek Trail/West Ridge couloir.

name: South Rib
beta: Initial pitches climb 4th-class rock with gear available in a central dihedral; higher pitches are dirt/tree/talus gullies broken by 3rd-class steps, commonly simul-climbed. Rock quality is intermittent throughout.
overview: Ascends Guye Peak's prominent, south-facing rib in five pitches of easy 5th-class rock and 3rd/4th-class scrambling, gradually easing toward the summit block.

current.approach: From I-90 Exit 52, follow Alpental Road up to the ski area and park at the Alpental ski-area lot (the Snow Lake trailhead parking) or in a legal spot along Alpental Road itself. The side roads named 'Strasse' are private, and since 2021 residents have barred climbers from driving or walking on them. For the south-face/rock routes, the crag rises directly above the parking area with essentially no approach hike required. For routes on other aspects of the mountain, use the Commonwealth Basin/PCT North Trailhead a short distance up the highway instead, following the Pacific Crest Trail into Commonwealth Basin before cutting up toward the peak. Because of the short, direct access, Guye Peak is climbed both summer and winter, though rock routes are primarily a snow-free-season (summer-fall) objective.
approach_variant_names: Sahale ski track and the south-side talus fans
current.descent: Rappelling the climb directly is difficult and largely requires downclimbing instead. The standard descent traverses north over Guye's subsummits, drops via a single rappel on established fixed tat into the Southeast Couloir, then climbs a steep gully back up to a notch before following the climbers' trail across toward Cave Ridge and down to the Snow Lake trailhead parking area.
current.detailed_rack: Single set of cams roughly 0.75-2 in (a central dihedral on the lower pitches is the main gear feature), a handful of slings for extension, and a single rope; no bolts/fixed anchors on route besides tat used at the SE Couloir rappel.
rack: Extra slings for extension (poor rock/pro quality)
current.pro_needs: A single rack of mostly cams from about 0.75 to 2 inches; small cracks are often dirt-filled and flaring so they take gear poorly. Carry extra slings to extend placements and cut rope drag on the wandering line.
current.rope_note: Guye Peak, Easy 5th class/Grade II, 800ft, 5 pitches. Single rack of cams .75-2in is sufficient; protection is intermittent/poor in dirty, flaring cracks, so bring extra slings to extend placements.

name: South Ridge
beta: From a camp at Wing Lake, hike around the lake and up a moraine onto a permanent snowfield to an obvious col in the south ridge. A broad, loose gully on the west side of the ridge leads up toward the final summit blocks, where several class-3 lines can be pieced together to a small, airy summit block reached via a ~100-ft, highly exposed knife-edge. The route is normally done without a rope. Rock is loose in many places, so care must be taken to avoid knocking rock onto climbers below.
overview: The South Ridge is Black Peak's original 1926 first-ascent line and remains the standard, easiest way to the 8,970 ft summit — a Grade II day combining talus-field hiking, a permanent snowfield, and class 3-4 rock scrambling above Wing Lake. It is one of the more accessible of Washington's 'Bulger' peaks (the state's 100 highest non-volcanic summits).

current.approach: Start at the Rainy Pass Picnic Area/Lake Ann trailhead on SR 20 (milepost ~157.5, elev. ~4,850 ft; 40-car lot with privy). Follow the Lake Ann/Maple Pass Trail (#740) about 1-1.5 miles to a signed junction and take the right fork toward Heather Pass (the left fork is the spur to Lake Ann). Climb through meadows to Heather Pass (~2.6 mi, ~6,100 ft), where the maintained trail ends. From the pass, pick up the unmarked climbers' path heading north, crossing two talus/boulder fields before dropping to Lewis Lake (~3.5-4 mi, ~5,700 ft; timbered campsites on the north side, water available) — this off-trail stretch is the main route-finding challenge of the approach, especially with cairns buried by early-season snow. From Lewis Lake, climb roughly 1,200 ft more of meadow and talus to Wing Lake (~5 mi, ~6,900 ft), the standard base camp, with sites in the trees on the right as you reach the lake and reliable water into late summer. From Wing Lake, go around the right (north) side of the lake and aim for the obvious talus/snow gully leading into the couloir just south of the summit; climb this gully, then angle climber's-right out of it to avoid cliff bands directly below the col, topping out at the south col on the crest of the south ridge — the true start of the climbing.
approach_variant_names: Rainy Pass and the Lake Ann/Maple Pass Trail to Heather Pass, then the unmarked path past Lewis Lake to Wing Lake
current.descent: This is the standard descent line for the peak — no separate down-route to learn. The ascent from the south col follows the cairned ridge (some class 3 moves) and a loose gully just west of the crest to the summit pyramid; the final section is a cairned class 2 ledge system traversing below the summit block that is exposed near its end, followed by a short (~15 ft) class 4 step to the true summit. On the way down, reverse this: downclimb the class 4 step (a boulder slung here permits a short optional rappel or hand-line — a single 30m rope is more than enough rope, and many parties skip the rope and downclimb it facing in), reverse the ledge traverse and the gully, and retrace the ridge back to the south col. From the col, descend the scree-and-snow slope (glissade-able early season) back down to Wing Lake, then hike out the approach trail. There is no mandatory multi-pitch rappel sequence on this route; the class 4 summit step is the only spot where climbers occasionally use a rope on the way down.
current.detailed_rack: No technical rack is needed for the standard route in normal (dry) conditions — this is an unroped class 2-4 scramble, climbed that way by several independent parties including a solo ascent in July 2017. Parties wanting extra security for the short exposed ridge traverse near the false summit, or for a steep snow section below the saddle in early season, sometimes carry a single ~30m rope with a very light rack. One 2017 group that carried light alpine racks with plenty of doubles left them mostly unused on the South Ridge portion of the day.
current.pro_needs: Protection is essentially unnecessary on this route — the main hazard is loose, rotten scree in the gully leading to the saddle (avoid party-inflicted rockfall), not a lack of gear. If roping up for the ~15-20m exposed knife-edge traverse near the true summit, slinging a horn or block is sufficient; no cam/nut rack is really needed.
current.rope_note: Most parties climb this route completely unroped (confirmed solo ascents in trip reports). If a rope is carried, a single 30m rope is plenty for the short exposed traverse near the false summit or a steep snow section below the saddle — descent is a walk-off down the same ridge, so no rappelling/double-rope length is needed.

name: South Ridge
beta: Pitch 1 climbs an obvious crack up the face to the 'U-notch' on the ridge; pitch 2 follows excellent cracks on the far side; pitches 3-4 are classic exposed knife-edge ridge ('B-Basin knife riding') ending in a short downclimb, after which the ridge broadens into mellow scrambling to the summit.
overview: A moderate 4-pitch rock line up Eldorado's south ridge — a crack system to a notch, then knife-edge ridge climbing — followed by broad, mellow scrambling to the true summit.

current.approach: From Seattle, drive I-5 north and then WA-20 (North Cascades Highway) east through Sedro-Woolley, Concrete, and Rockport to Marblemount, then follow Cascade River Road south for about 20 miles — paved for the first 10 miles, gravel and washboard the rest of the way — to the Eldorado parking area near mile 20. From the trailhead, hikers backtrack a short distance along the road to find a safe crossing of the Cascade River (historically a large log or braided ford, which shifts year to year), then pick up a steep, unmaintained climbers' boot path that gains roughly 3,000-3,500 feet through old-growth forest to a boulder field, crosses Eldorado Creek, and opens into the alpine meadows of the Eldorado Creek basin, a common camp area roughly 5-6 hours from the car. From the basin, the route continues onto glaciated terrain (roped travel and crevasse-rescue gear required) to the high camp near 7,600 ft on the Inspiration Glacier flat. Any overnight stay requires a free North Cascades National Park backcountry permit — Eldorado is managed as a high-use cross-country zone with advance reservations available on Recreation.gov plus a limited walk-up allocation issued in person at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center. For this specific route: from high camp, traverse the steep, exposed snow on the flank of the glacier (crampons mandatory) to the lowest point of the south ridge, the left-hand skyline seen from camp, below an obvious crack leading up to a U-shaped notch in the crest.
approach_variant_names: Glacier flank traverse from the east ridge camp
current.descent: Descend via Eldorado's standard East Ridge route back toward the glacier camp.
current.detailed_rack: A single rack to 2 inches covers the crack pitches.
current.pro_needs: Standard trad protection to 2 inches for the crack-and-ridge pitches.
bivy: Marble Creek Campground, Cascade River Road

name: South Ridge
