beta: Approach as for Forbidden Peak from low camp (5,300 ft) or high camp (6,400 ft). Navigate toward South Ridge approach facing Forbidden Glacier. Route-finding less obvious than North Ridge; scout carefully. Follow exposed ridge combining fourth-class scrambling with short pitches of 5.6 climbing.
overview: A cool 5.6 romp up exposed ridge combining fourth-class scrambling with short 5th-class sections. Similar commitment to North Ridge but slightly more technical. Half-day alpine objective from Boston Basin camps.

current.approach: From Seattle, drive I-5 north to Burlington, then WA-20 east through Marblemount, and turn onto Cascade River Road, following its paved-then-gravel surface about 21.7 miles to a small pullout at 3,200 ft that marks the unmaintained Boston Basin Trailhead (a different stop, a couple of miles up-road of the Eldorado trailhead, and just before the road's end at Cascade Pass). From there a steep, unmaintained climbers' path follows the old Diamond Mine roadbed briefly before climbing hard, crossing several streams, and breaking above treeline (~5,300 ft) to reach the popular Boston Basin high camp around 6,400 ft — roughly 3-4 miles one-way with about 3,000-3,300 ft of elevation gain. From camp, West Ridge climbers continue cross-country over the glacier to a couloir that gains the ridge crest. Because Boston Basin is a high-demand cross-country camping zone in North Cascades National Park, overnight parties need a wilderness permit; a portion of peak-season (mid-May to mid-October) slots can be reserved in advance via Recreation.gov's early-access lottery, with the remainder issued as limited first-come, first-served walk-up permits. For this specific route: from Boston Basin high camp, a short approach up into the Forbidden Peak zone reaches this minor summit; North and South Ridge differ only in which side of the formation is climbed from the same camp.
approach_variant_names: Boston Basin high camp
current.descent: Descend the North Ridge: make one rappel of about 40 ft from fixed slings, then downclimb the rest of that ridge and return to camp.
current.detailed_rack: A light alpine rack covers this route: a single set of cams from finger-size up to about 2in, with doubles in the common 0.5-1in range for the sustained low-5th ridge climbing and the 5.6 crux on pitch 3 (bypassing a gendarme on the right, on more solid but harder rock). Bring a set of stoppers/nuts too — the ridge is described as loose and lichen-covered in places, so smaller opportunistic nut/cam placements matter as much as a big piece. There is no fixed protection on-route except a single faded rap sling at the P2/P3 notch belay below the gendarme.
current.pro_needs: Protection is moderate but not continuous — this is a broken, sometimes loose ridge crest rather than a clean crack system, so gear comes from natural placements as terrain allows rather than a splitter line. There is an abundance of loose, lichen-y rock, and belayers on pitch 2 should stay out of the fall line because of rockfall risk from parties above on the pitch 3 crux.
current.rope_note: Standard multi-pitch 5.6 alpine granite route in Boston Basin; well-protected cracks/corners take a light alpine rack.

name: Southeast Face
beta: Pitch 1 steps onto a detached block, then works up a widening finger-to-ring-lock seam that zig-zags just left of the arete to a two-bolt anchor in a notch (no chains/rings). Pitch 2 traverses left from the belay past two bolts, then follows a 'choose your own adventure' line up the face, with gear mostly limited to thin cracks and horizontal seams; the upper section has some lichen.
overview: A harder, more sustained alternative to the classic Southeast Ridge, climbing the exposed granite face directly right of the ridge crest in 2 pitches up to 5.10-. First climbed in September 1990 by Jim Nelson, Jim Martin, Kit Lewis, Bill Liddell, and Dave Bale, it shares the Southeast Ridge's approach via Boston Basin and the Quien Sabe Glacier but sees far fewer ascents.

current.approach: Drive Cascade River Road roughly 21.7 miles from Marblemount to the small, unsigned Boston Basin pulloff/trailhead at about 3,200-3,300 ft (a rough, sometimes rutted gravel road best driven with a bit of clearance). From the trailhead, follow the old abandoned mining road for about 0.75 mile to a derelict mine site, where the road ends and an unmaintained but well-traveled climbers' boot path takes over. This path climbs steeply through forest, crossing four small streams/seasonal creeks (reliable water in early/mid season, so top off bottles here), and reaches treeline around 5,300 ft after roughly 2.5-3 miles and about 3,000 ft of gain. Low camp sits on heather benches around 5,300-5,700 ft; a higher camp on a knoll above green meadows at roughly 6,300-6,400 ft cuts real time off summit day. From high camp, contour up open talus and slabs to the western edge of the Quien Sabe Glacier below Sharkfin Col. Rope up for glacier travel and traverse east along the top of the glacier several hundred feet to the base of the gully/couloir below the tower - if a bergschrund or seracs bar the direct line, class 3-4 slabs on the left provide an alternate entry, rejoining the couloir about 100 ft up. Getting into the correct gully matters: on July 10, 2005, a six-person Mountaineers party mistakenly climbed a similar-looking but incorrect gully here; during the roped traverse back toward the standard line a climber was struck by rockfall, and minutes later, during the retreat rappel, a natural boulder anchor gave way, killing three and seriously injuring a fourth, so confirm the line (ideally with GPS track or beta photos) before committing, especially in poor visibility. For the Southeast Face specifically, there is no separate approach line to the face itself - parties climb the first two pitches of the Southeast Ridge (the block/dihedral pitch to the notch, described in that route) and rappel from a fixed anchor at the top of pitch 2 to reach the base of the Southeast Face's crack pitch. In July the bottom of the approach gully is guarded by a moat, and a short wall of snow must be climbed to reach the chute.
approach_variant_names: The correct gully off the Quien Sabe, then two pitches of the Southeast Ridge and a rappel to reach the face
current.descent: Descent is a combination of short technical rappels off the face followed by the shared Sharkfin descent gully used by all routes on the tower. From the top of the Southeast Face's second pitch, make two 75-foot (~23m) rappels back down to the notch atop Southeast Ridge pitch 1/2 - a single 60m rope doubled is more than adequate for both. The anchors here are bolted but sparse: the two-bolt station at the top of pitch 1 has no chains or rap rings, so plan to leave a locking biner, rap ring, or short cord unless you can retrieve gear on the way down; there is no anchor at the very base of pitch 1, so keep the team roped/attentive on that stretch. Once back at the ridge notch, continue down via the same downclimb-and-rappel gully system used to descend the Southeast Ridge (see that route's descent for detail) - expect several more short rappels on natural anchors (chockstones, boulders, occasional slung horns) interspersed with 3rd/4th-class downclimbing, dropping back onto the Quien Sabe Glacier and the walk back to camp. Loose rock in this gully is a real hazard, and this is where a well-documented, fatal accident occurred on July 10, 2005 (a party that had mistakenly entered this gully was retreating when a natural boulder anchor gave way about 10 feet into the rappel, sending three climbers and the boulder roughly 300 ft down the gully and killing them), so back up questionable anchors, rappel one at a time where the gully is confined, and don't over-trust a single boulder or flake. In July the last rappel down the gully wall is about 30 m and lands at a moat, so a doubled 60 m rope helps clear it.
current.detailed_rack: Single light rack to about 2 inches (thin-to-mid cams and small nuts) plus extra slings; the route relies on four fixed bolts (two at the P1 belay/notch anchor, which has no chains or rings, and two on the P2 face traverse) supplemented by natural gear in seams and horizontal breaks.
current.pro_needs: Good protection low on P1 once the seam widens past fingers to ring-locks, but sparse and thin higher on P2's face — look for horizontal seams and thin cracks. The P1 bolted anchor lacks chains/rings, so plan to leave a nut or sling to retreat, and the unhangered bolt at the P1 base needs a supplemental gear anchor for the belayer.
bivy: Informal snow and rock bivouacs above the basins
current.rope_note: 2 pitches, ~150ft total (5.10-, Grade II). Descent is two 75ft rappels from a fixed anchor at the top.

name: West Ridge (Beckey Route)
beta: The standard/easiest way up Hard Mox: from a high camp near the Redoubt Glacier/Depot-Redoubt divide, traverse the glacier to the saddle between the Mox Peaks and Mt. Redoubt, descend into the 'Col of the Wild,' gain the Ridge of Gendarmes, then follow ledge/gully systems (West Ledges, Gendarme Notch, East Ledges, Southeast Gullies) to a high notch just left of the summit tower. From the notch, three pitches of loose 4th-to-low-5th-class climbing lead to the top. Most of the climbing looks more intimidating than it is; if the climbing feels harder than 5.5, you are probably off route. The route is not sandbagged but is terrifically chossy.
overview: Southeast Mox Peak ("Hard Mox," 8,504 ft) is the true, higher summit of the Twin Spires and is generally regarded as the hardest peak on Washington's Bulger List (100 highest summits) and one of the state's "Difficult Ten." This standard route climbs from the Col of the Wild — the notch separating Hard Mox from Northwest/Easy Mox — over the Ridge of Gendarmes and up a loose gully system to a notch on the peak's west side, then three roped pitches (up to 5.5, easing to sparse-pro Class 4 near the top) to the summit. The peak's own west-ridge line was first climbed in 1941 by a Fred Beckey party; that route saw its first winter ascent in December 2023 (Eric Gilbertson and Nick Roy, 5 pitches WI2 M5 with rime-covered rock, ~18-hour summit push).

current.approach: From the Depot Creek trailhead parking on the abandoned logging spur off Chilliwack Lake Road (BC) at roughly 2,350 ft, hike the old roadway grade uphill (left-hand fork) for about a mile to the Monument 65 border marker, where you cross into North Cascades National Park and should sign in at the wilderness-permit kiosk. From there the route follows the unmaintained, unmarked 'Depot Creek climbers path' — a boot-track through old-growth forest for roughly 3 miles that gains to the base of Depot Creek Falls (about 4.8 hours and 1,600 ft in from the cars). The falls are one of the tallest in Washington (drop cited around 900-1,000 ft), and the path climbs steep, often wet and slippery slabs along its left edge; a fixed handline is present at the crux scramble section here and this is the approach's main technical hazard (exposed, greasy rock, worse in the wet or in the dark — several parties report losing the tread here at night). Above the falls the path eases through scrubby subalpine forest onto a broad outwash plain, reaching treeline where climbers typically switch to mountaineering boots/crampons. Continue up class 3 tread gaining roughly 800 ft into the Redoubt Glacier basin; Ouzel Lake, in this basin, is the most common first camp. From Ouzel Lake most parties relocate camp 3-4 hours further up onto the Redoubt Glacier saddle/col (~7,150 ft) for a high camp closer to the peaks — this leg is flat glacier travel with only minor, usually avoidable crevasse hazard in normal late-season conditions. From high camp, traverse roughly 2 miles east across snow/glacier beneath Easy Mox's south side toward the 'Col of the Wild,' the saddle between Easy and Hard (Southeast) Mox, finishing with a steep ~1,000 ft climb over notoriously unstable, sandy talus (loose rock is the dominant hazard on this whole upper approach — helmets on well before the col). From the Col of the Wild, ascend a ramp leading right past a snow patch into a gully, then scramble up and right (class 4, exposed enough that many parties belay it) toward a notch in the 'Ridge of Gendarmes.' A short sequence of ledges zig-zagging right-left-right leads through the notch; descend briefly to a small flat area and locate the correct gully leading to a high notch on the west ridge, which is the start of the roped climbing (two pitches of 5th class to the summit tower, then a final short, exposed class 3 scramble — stay roped — to the true summit). Water is available from the glacier/snowmelt and Ouzel Lake but not reliably along the upper ridge, so carry enough from camp.
approach_variant_names: Depot Creek from the north side of the border to the lake camp
Two camps: the lake basin or the glacier saddle above it
current.descent: Descend by reversing the ascent line rather than any independent walk-off. From the true summit, most parties make three single-rope (30 m) rappels down the tower to a small, exposed high notch, then one longer double-rope (60 m) rappel from that notch down into the gully/glacier below — roughly four rappels in typical late-summer, snow-free conditions. Anchors along this line are almost entirely improvised rather than bolted: slung boulders, horns and pedestals wrapped with tat/cord, and the occasional jammed knot in a crack; a couple of the stations have accumulated enough old cord to look semi-permanent, but none should be trusted blindly and back-up/extend as needed. Bring a single 60 m rope (or two ropes if you want to do the notch-to-glacier drop as one clean pull rather than downclimbing part of it). In seasons or conditions where a snow finger lingers in the descent gully, parties have needed far more — up to 9-10 shorter single-rope rappels interspersed with downclimbing to get through the same 400-ft gully system, because a lingering snow patch prevents a clean full-length pull; budget extra time and a plan B if you find snow still choking the gully. Known hazards on this descent: persistently loose, choss-prone rock (the Southeast Spire's rock quality is poor, and at least one incident involved a slab breaking loose during rope retrieval at the notch and striking a climber), ropes getting stuck when pulled through the loose gully, high exposure along the east ledges near the Ridge of Gendarmes, and fatigue/darkness on the lower-angle terrain given how long this climb runs. After reaching the glacier below the Col of the Wild, reverse the approach traverse back to your high camp (Redoubt Col/Ouzel Lake), then descend the Depot Creek climbers path past the falls — using the fixed handline again on the steep slab section — back to the trailhead.
current.detailed_rack: Alpine rock rack with cams, nuts, and slings; bring a rope for the technical sections and rappel descent.
current.pro_needs: Sustained exposed climbing to 5.6 on a long rib; a standard alpine rack and rope are needed for the crux and rappels.

name: Southeast Ridge (SE Corner)
beta: Grade 5.3-5.7, II-III Alpine. 600 vertical feet over 6 pitches from ridge base to summit. Rock quality excellent. Primary hazards: high exposure, significant glacier crevasses, late-season ice conditions, Class 4 downclimbing. 60m rope required for descent rappels. Accessible via Sulphide Glacier or Fisher Chimneys approaches. Often requires bivy camp due to multi-day approach.
overview: The classic technical finish to Shuksan's Summit Pyramid, climbed after approaching via Fisher Chimneys or Sulphide Glacier: six pitches of good-quality rock up to 5.3 gaining the pyramid's SE corner.

current.approach: East-northeast up Shannon Ridge, then traverse Sulphide Glacier to reach southeast ridge base By mid-August one stretch of the forest road to the Shannon Ridge trailhead is washed out and high clearance helps; the trail up the ridge is cleared and easy to follow, and the glacier's lowest slope is hard ice at dawn after a cold night, with crevasses right away and no set bootpack. In mid-June the snow is continuous from about 4,700 ft and the basin camp near 6,200 ft has running water and dry pads; slopes above camp can shed wet avalanches onto the trail on the way out.
approach_variant_names: Shannon Ridge and the Sulphide Glacier to the notch on the southeast ridge
Lake Ann and the Fisher Chimneys to the summit pyramid
current.descent: Rappel the same 4th-class gully used as the standard ascent line up the summit pyramid (the line shared with the Fisher Chimneys/Sulphide Glacier finish); a 60m rope reaches all belay stations.
current.detailed_rack: A light trad rack suffices: double-length slings for the ridge, small-to-medium nuts and cams to about 1.5 inches (tricams work well), plus full glacier travel and crevasse-rescue gear for the approach.
current.pro_needs: Protection is mostly for the last three low-5th-class pitches; gear to 1.5 inches with extra slings covers it.
bivy: Shannon Ridge crest camps, below the park boundary
current.rope_note: Only the final ~600 ft above the notch is technical; class 3 approach pitches often simul-hiked or unroped. Selective route-finding keeps hardest moves at 5.3-5.4.

name: Southern Man
beta: Starts up the Direct East Buttress, busting left of its bolt-ladder pitch onto a funky 5.10a section; rock quality improves through the headwall pitches, which feature sustained thin cracks starting in a corner and staying difficult for several pitches; the crux is an 5.11d pitch near the route's end. Belay locations are described as somewhat ambiguous/unmarked in the field.
overview: Named after the Neil Young song, Southern Man splits off from the Direct East Buttress about halfway up and climbs the south-facing headwall on SEWS's upper south side to the summit. First ascended by Mark Allen, Joel Kauffman, and Leaghan Falley, August 2008 (aided at 5.9+ C1); freed by B. Matthews and Bryan Burdo in 2010 at 5.11d (a September 2009 ascent by Burdo at 5.12a is unconfirmed).

current.approach: Same as Direct East Buttress: park at the hairpin pullout on Highway 20, hike Spire Gully (cairned) to the last large tree, traverse right across talus/snow to the gully leading to the notch between North and South Early Winters Spire, then traverse left to the base of the east buttress. Southern Man shares the East Buttress's first pitches, then splits off around halfway up to climb the south-facing headwall on the upper south side of the peak for its final 5 pitches (9 total) to the top.
approach_variant_names: The hairpin pullout and Spire Gully to the last large tree, then right across the talus toward the inter-spire notch
current.descent: From the summit, take the standard South Arete descent: downclimb the arete (3rd/4th class with a short, more exposed 5th-class section) to the Rabbit Ears, then 3 single-rope rappels (60m rope) from bolted anchors/chains down the gully to the base. Note that the belays on Southern Man itself are vague and not yet equipped with fixed anchors — this affects the climb, not the descent, but underscores that this route sees less traffic than the East Buttress it starts from, so don't expect a fully bolted rap line down the route itself if you need to bail from the upper headwall; natural anchors would be required there.
current.detailed_rack: Standard alpine trad rack with an emphasis on thin gear (small cams/nuts) for the sustained thin-crack pitches; bring extra slings for the unfixed upper belays.
rack: Single 60m rope for the lead and the rappels
current.pro_needs: Trad protection throughout; belay stances on some pitches are unfixed.
current.rope_note: Sustained 9-pitch 5.11d testpiece on SEWS; full rack plus extra small cams for sustained crux pitches.

name: Southwest Buttress
beta: A 9-pitch, III, 5.8 alpine rock route established around 1985, rising in a continuous, blocky, bent line from the small glacier shared with Early Morning Spire to the summit, reached via a long glaciated approach from the Eldorado trailhead.
overview: The Southwest Buttress is Dorado Needle's longest and most sustained rock route: over 1,000 ft (9 pitches) of quality granite up steep cracks and slabs, past photogenic gendarmes, to an airy knife-edge summit ridge. Rated Grade III, 5.8, it's a popular objective in its own right, reached via the same Eldorado-area glacier approach used for Eldorado Peak and the East Ridge.

current.approach: The hike-in to the Southwest Buttress follows the identical trailhead-to-glacier approach as the East Ridge: from the Eldorado Trailhead on Cascade River Road, cross the Cascade River/Eldorado Creek near the parking area (backtrack downstream to find a log or ford), pick up the climbers' path on the west side of Eldorado Creek, and climb steeply through old-growth forest (no water on this stretch) to a talus field around 4,000 ft. Re-cross Eldorado Creek near a cairn at about 5,100 ft, switchback up past 6,000 ft, and drop via a short Class 3 gully into Roush Creek basin (6,100-6,400 ft, reliable water, a good lower camp/bail-out point). From the basin, ascend 20-30-degree snow onto the toe of the Eldorado Glacier at about 7,500 ft - rope up for crevasse hazard from here on - and establish a high camp on rock/moraine near the glacier shoulder for the multi-day stay. Where the Southwest Buttress approach diverges is the final glacier traverse: from camp, continue across the Inspiration Glacier and over onto the McAllister Glacier, heading toward the Marble Creek-McAllister pass. The base of the Southwest Buttress is reached via a prominent gully - often snow-filled year-round - that begins roughly 700 vertical feet below that pass and drops to the toe of the buttress on the peak's southwest side.
approach_variant_names: Marble Creek-McAllister pass, then 700 ft down to the snow gully at the toe
current.descent: From the summit, downclimb/scramble a short distance to a large rock/boulder on the ridge about 10 meters north of the true summit, where a fixed rappel ring and sling (recently reported as reinforced with an additional sling) anchors the route's single rappel: a double-rope rappel (both strands, ~60m rope) that lowers you to a steep snow slope which, in normal-season conditions, keeps a solid connection to the rock, so a moat crossing usually isn't required at this point. From the bottom of that rappel, downclimb/glissade the snow slope to the notch at the base of the route - the same notch used on the approach - and reverse the glacier travel back toward camp. Some parties describe an alternate single-rope-length rappel off the top of the summit gully instead of the ridge-boulder station; functionally this is still a one-rappel descent, just from a slightly different anchor. Either way, plan on exactly one rope-length transition, not a multi-pitch rappel sequence - the rest of the descent is downclimbing, scrambling, and glacier travel. Because this is a moderate Grade III+ route rather than a big-wall-style descent, no v-thread or chained-rappel sequence is needed in summer conditions; the main descent hazard is the moat at the base of the route staying open or widening late in the season, which can complicate reconnecting with the glacier.
current.detailed_rack: Single rack of cams to #3 Camalot (rarely need the #3) with doubles in 0.5, 0.75, and 1 inch, plus a set of nuts; natural gear anchors are used throughout — no fixed anchors on route except the rappel station near the summit.
current.pro_needs: Good crack systems take cams well throughout; doubles in the 0.5-1" range cover most placements.
bivy: Marble Creek Campground, Cascade River Road

name: Soviet Route
beta: The 1975 first-ascent party climbed the buttress in 22 pitches over three days using titanium pitons and early Abalakov-style protection; a 2012 ascent using modern gear and 200-ft ropes compressed it to roughly 14 pitches plus 4 belay moves. The route features a major horizontal ledge at half height that is key to the line, a cave belay mid-crux, and three consecutive pitches near 5.10a/b as the technical crux, with much of the remainder in the 5.6-5.9 range. Rock is meta-granitic but includes sections of loose red rock; that party took just under 12 hours from the buttress base to the Southwest Peak. A long route (14 pitches of full 60m/200ft length on the 2012 ascent; the 1975 FA logged 22 pitches).
overview: The Soviet Route (aka the West Buttress) climbs a roughly 2,300-foot buttress on Bonanza's Southwest Peak (9,320'), a distinct sub-summit south of Bonanza's true 9,516' main summit. First climbed September 10-12, 1975 by a joint Soviet-American team during a Cold War-era climbing exchange — one of the first times Soviet climbers had climbed in the U.S. — it remains one of the most historically significant big alpine rock routes in the North Cascades: serious, remote, and rarely repeated (only a handful of documented ascents) given its length and variable rock quality.

current.approach: From Holden Village, follow the Railroad Creek Trail (FST 1256) west about 3.5 miles to Hart Lake (3,956'), passing (but not taking) the Holden Lake Trail junction along the way — stay on the main valley trail. At Hart Lake, leave the maintained trail and climb the rock-and-heather terraces on the true left (west) side of the drainage below Bonanza's massive west-facing buttress: roughly 3,000' of gain in about three hours of steep, routefinding-heavy travel — open forest giving way to heather benches and then blocky, loose terrain — to reach a camp near the 7,100' col/pass between North Star Mountain and Bonanza's Southwest Peak. Water is available at Hart Lake and again at the camp near the pass (snowmelt/tarns), but is scarce on the terrace climb between them, so fill up at both. There is no trail above Hart Lake; the terrace system requires real routefinding judgment, and the lower slopes hold loose rock and brush that make the approach itself a meaningful crux before the technical climbing starts.
approach_variant_names: Railroad Creek Trail to Hart Lake, then the terraces to the North Star-Bonanza col
current.descent: From the Southwest Peak (route's high point), traverse the Northeast Ridge to the West Peak — about 2 hours, negotiating a series of gendarmes mostly on 3rd/4th-class ledges, with one short rappel along the way. From the West Peak, descend the northwest side: downclimb talus, then make two rappels of roughly 200 feet each down steep slabs back into the approach basin. Anchors on this descent have historically been improvised rather than fixed — one documented descent used a nut at the top station and a piton at the lower one — so carry a small rack/cordage to build or reinforce anchors rather than counting on hardware being in place. Two 200-ft rappels require a rope of at least 60m (or two ropes joined) to reach each next stance without coming up short. Parties have finished this descent after dark on long summit days, so budget extra time and bring a headlamp. From the bottom of the raps, continue downclimbing talus back to camp near the 7,100' pass, then reverse the terrace descent to Hart Lake and the Railroad Creek Trail back to Holden.
current.detailed_rack: Cams doubled in the finger-to-hand sizes (small Aliens most useful; one repeat ascent found the #3 and #4 unnecessary), a full set of nuts and small wires, a couple of thin knifeblade pitons (optional, for old fixed placements), and twin 60 m ropes for double-rope technique.
rack: Cams, doubles finger-to-hand sizes (small Aliens most useful), plus #3/#4
current.pro_needs: Protection is generally good with cams and nuts on the more solid sections; be selective and test placements on the loose red rock bands noted by repeat ascent parties.
bivy: High camp near North Star-Bonanza pass (~7,100 ft)
current.rope_note: 22-pitch route on the North Face/West Buttress of Bonanza's SW peak. One modern ascent used two 60m ropes with both followers belayed simultaneously for full 200-ft pitches; two 200-ft (60m) rappels used on descent.

name: West Route
beta: Most parties approach via Phelps Creek Trail to Leroy Basin, cross the Leroy High Route to Ice Lakes, camp at Lower or Upper Ice Lake, then descend and traverse into the basin between North and South Spectacle Butte before climbing the Southwest Ridge to the south summit. The line is a straightforward Class 3 ridge scramble, but the ridge crest is broken by loose gendarmes that force route-finding onto ledges and a short chossy chute/dike passage that some parties rate closer to Class 4.
overview: A pair of pyramidal twin summits in the Entiat Mountains subrange of the North Cascades, within the Glacier Peak Wilderness on Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest (Wenatchee River Ranger District) land in Chelan County. The sharper south summit (8,392 ft) is the true high point; the north butte (8,080 ft) sits about a half-mile away across a connecting basin. The name comes from their twin-lensed profile as seen from the Entiat River valley. First ascent of the south peak was made August 20, 1953 by Rowland Tabor and Dwight Crowder. This route follows the southwest ridge/west-facing slopes — the standard line on South Spectacle Butte — reached via a long, mostly cross-country approach through Leroy Basin and the Ice Lakes basin. Traffic is light; most parties combine it with Ice Lakes camping or a Leroy-Carne loop.

current.approach: The standard approach is a long, mostly cross-country line from the Phelps Creek Trailhead at the end of Phelps Creek Road (FR 6211), about 3,500 ft. Follow Phelps Creek Trail #1511 up the east side of the valley — a gentle, well-graded grade of roughly 275 ft per mile — crossing into the Glacier Peak Wilderness at 2.6 miles and reaching the Leroy Creek ford at about 3.5 miles. Immediately across the ford, the unmaintained Leroy Creek high route (Trail #1512) branches steeply north-east; it is well trodden but climbs at roughly 1,200 ft per mile for about 1.5 miles into Leroy Basin, where established camps sit off a steep path above the creek crossing. This half is hot and exposed under an overnight pack, so carry several liters. Campfires are prohibited above 5,000 ft anywhere in the wilderness, and a free self-issue wilderness permit is filled out at the trailhead. From camp, pick up the Carne Mountain high trail — an old sheepherder track — and follow it south-east, giving up a little elevation to cross the south fork of Leroy Creek before climbing to the 6,850 ft saddle at Leroy Pass; cairns mark the way but several paths braid apart in the basin, so stay on the lower and better-trodden line where they diverge. Continue east on faint footpaths through heather, then talus and scree, gaining about 750 ft over roughly a mile to Freezer Pass at 7,600 ft. There is no maintained tread here and the bootpaths come and go, so keep track of your line for the return; snow can linger on this stretch into early or mid July. Drop north-east off the pass down talus into the Ice Lakes basin, passing the north end of Upper Ice Lake and following the dry stream bed to the west shore of Lower Ice Lake. Both lakes are reliable water. Pick up the faint remnants of the historic Ice Lakes Trail on the north side and sidehill east at about 6,600 ft on slippery scrub and loose rock with no real tread — keep the party strung out in a line rather than stacked one above another, because almost everything here moves underfoot. Roughly a third of a mile brings you to the lip of a washed-out gully; downclimb the loose clay and scree into it and climb the far side back to about the same elevation, picking the crossing line carefully, since dropping too low can leave you cliffed out. This is the last reliable water before the summit. Beyond it the traverse eases into the open basin floor between the two Buttes at about 6,800 ft, where a scree-and-talus ramp gains the crest of the southwest ridge and the scrambling begins. A separate approach corridor exists on the west side of the peak: leaving Phelps Creek Trail #1511 at around 5,300 ft and climbing cross-country east through heather and talus benches to gain the peak's west-facing slopes. It is a shorter day from the trailhead and avoids the Freezer Pass crossing, but it is a different line from the one this route's waypoints and descent follow, and the north side of that ridge is cliffy and should not be entered.
approach_variant_names: Phelps Creek and Leroy Basin over Leroy and Freezer passes to the Ice Lakes basin
current.descent: There is no rappelling on this route and no shortcut descent gully — it is a walk-off and downclimb by the line used on the ascent. From the 8,392 ft summit, reverse the ledges on the south-east corner of the summit block back onto the crest of the southwest ridge at about 8,100 ft; the cairns here blend into the surrounding rock and are easy to lose, so pick the line up deliberately rather than drifting down the first ledge system that goes. Downclimb the crest on Class 2-3 talus and broken rock, turning the gendarmes on climber's right as you did on the way up, and reverse the crux at around 7,700 ft — the Class 3 dike, the traverse on down-sloping rock, and the short chossy chute — facing in, one at a time, on rotten holds with real exposure. Below the gendarmes, descend the scree-and-talus ramp roughly 400 ft into the open basin floor between the two Buttes. From there retrace the traverse west: cross the washed-out gully at about 6,600 ft, keeping the party strung out in a line rather than stacked, and sidehill back across the loose scrub and rock to the west shore of Lower Ice Lake. Regain the faint remnants of the old Ice Lakes Trail, climb back up the talus to Freezer Pass at 7,600 ft, then follow the faint heather-and-scree footpaths west over Leroy Pass at 6,850 ft and down the Carne Mountain high trail into Leroy Basin camp. The bootpaths between the passes come and go, so the return is materially easier if you tracked your line on the way in. From camp, reverse the steep unmaintained Leroy Creek high route to the ford and follow Phelps Creek Trail #1511 back down-valley to the trailhead. The hazards on the whole descent are rockfall, loose downsloping rock on the ridge, and losing the cairned or booted line in scree and talus — not rope work. An alternate exit some parties use drops west off the peak's west-facing slopes through heather and talus to rejoin Phelps Creek Trail #1511 directly at around 5,300 ft, avoiding the return over Freezer and Leroy Passes; it is a different line from the ascent, it leaves any camp at Ice Lakes or Leroy Basin behind you, and the north side of that ridge is cliffy and should not be entered, so treat it as a deliberate choice made in advance rather than a shortcut taken on the descent.
current.detailed_rack: No fixed protection exists on this scramble route. Some parties carry a short rope and a small rack/slings as a safety margin for the class 3 ledge/gully step near the gendarme, though most climb it unroped.
current.pro_needs: No fixed protection is placed; this is an unroped scramble on loose rock, though some parties carry a short rope/harness for the exposed traverse near the second spire as a precaution.
current.rope_note: Entiat Mountains. Southwest ridge line; Class 2-3 with a short, exposed Class 3 crux near 7,700 ft that most parties climb unroped.

name: South Ridge ("Spirited Away")
beta: The South Ridge ("Spirited Away", IV 5.9, established by Sam Boyce & Joe Manning, July 2022) climbs 12 pitches up Spectre's south ridge from Pickle Pass: sustained 5.4-5.8 crest climbing past an overhanging 5.9R choss crux (P3), through a shattered gendarme requiring a short rappel-and-reclimb (P7), and finishing through narrow hoodoo towers before a ~30m rappel and a 600-ft scramble to the summit.
overview: Spectre Peak (7,952'; a LIDAR-based figure gives 7,953') sits on the western slope of the Northern Pickets — it's grouped thematically with neighboring Ghost Peak and Phantom Peak near Swiss Peak and Mount Challenger, part of the Northern Pickets traverse line (Luna-Fury-Swiss-Spectre-Phantom-Crooked Thumb-Ghost-Challenger). It is one of the most remote and rarely climbed summits in the Pickets, with only two documented technical routes on record: Haunted Wall (IV 5.9+, 2,100', Wayne Wallace and Mike Layton, Aug 2006) and this South Ridge line.

current.approach: Start at the Hannegan Pass Trailhead (elev. ~3,120 ft) at the end of Ruth Creek Road (FS-32). From the trailhead, follow the maintained Hannegan Pass Trail #674 gently up the Ruth Creek valley (views of Mt. Sefrit and Nooksack Ridge) for about 4 miles and roughly 2,000 ft of gain to 5,050 ft Hannegan Pass — this stretch is straightforward, well-graded, and has reliable water at Ruth Creek crossings for the first couple of miles. From the pass, stay on the maintained trail as it drops past Boundary Camp and Copper Creek Camp into the Chilliwack valley; roughly two miles beyond Copper Creek an easily missed side path leads down to the Chilliwack River ford (about 2,750 ft), and the Easy Ridge path climbs steeply from the far bank. From here it is sustained, largely cross-country travel: climb onto and follow Easy Ridge itself, a hot, dry, open, south-facing ridge crest with limited shade — flowing water is available relatively early on the ridge but the FA party warned it becomes brutal later in the season and in dry years. Continue along/over Easy Peak (a common first bivy, roughly a full day, ~10 hours, from the trailhead) and then descend/traverse past the notch known as Imperfect Impasse, before regaining elevation to Challenger Col on the flank of Mt. Challenger. From Challenger Col, traverse the southern Challenger cirque (glacial terrain — rope/crevasse-awareness recommended near the pocket glacier) toward the west ridge of Phantom Peak, a typical second bivy site, avoiding lingering snow at Pickle Pass. From this high camp it is a further, mostly straightforward cross-country traverse across the western slopes to the base of Spectre Peak's south ridge, reached around sunrise on what is effectively day three. In total this is roughly a 46-mile, ~17,500 ft round-trip approach-and-climb outing (74 km), typically broken into 2 or more travel days each way with route-finding, glacier travel, and off-trail ridge scrambling throughout — this is genuinely one of the longest, most remote approaches in the North Cascades, not a simple hike-in.
approach_variant_names: Hannegan Pass, Easy Ridge and Challenger Col
current.descent: The descent does not reverse the ridge. Both of the route's rappels — about 25 m into the gap at the Pitch 7 gendarme and about 30 m off the final hoodoo tower — are made on the way up, below the last ~600 ft of scrambling to the top, so a single 60 m rope covers them. No fixed anchors are documented on this obscure, first-ascent-era route; expect natural gear anchors (horns, cracks, slung blocks) rather than bolts, and back them up — this is remote, low-traffic terrain with essentially no fixed hardware. From the summit, the descent drops onto Spectre's east-facing slopes back toward the Challenger Col/Easy Ridge approach line; in the FA party's heavy-snow-year, early-season conditions this was continuous, relaxed steep snow (glissade-friendly with an ice axe and the usual steep-snow/glacier caution), letting them avoid the usual endless scree and loose talus that this face otherwise holds in leaner, later-season conditions — parties visiting in a low-snow year or later in the season should expect a much looser, scree/talus descent instead of snow travel. From the base, retrace the approach line back over Challenger Col, past Imperfect Impasse, along Easy Ridge, over Hannegan Pass, and out the maintained trail to the Hannegan Pass Trailhead — effectively a full reversal of the multi-day approach, not a same-day walk-off.
current.detailed_rack: Single 60m rope; singles of cams from about 0.1-2 (BD C4-equivalent sizing), doubles of 0.3-1, an optional #3, a light set of nuts, and roughly 50 ft of cord/webbing for slinging horns and chockstones.
current.pro_needs: No detailed rack has been published. The FA account notes loose rock requiring 'creative anchor construction,' so plan on a standard alpine rock rack with extra small-to-mid cams and slings for improvised gear anchors rather than relying on fixed protection.
bivy: Easy Ridge bivouac ground below Easy Peak
Improvised bivouacs on the Challenger Glacier and the crest south of Challenger
Perfect Pass, Perfect Pass cross-country zone
current.rope_note: Northern Pickets, remote south face/ridge route: 12 pitches of ridge climbing with two short rappels on the way up (about 25 m and 30 m), which a single 60 m rope covers.

name: East Face (2002)
beta: Starts with two pitches on the slabby face just left of a small, deteriorating pocket glacier under the large gully on the east face. Above the slab, the face forces you left over a small rock wall, then continues straight up for a couple more pitches through brush and small trees. The route then narrows and traverses right on a narrow, jungle-filled ledge with significant exposure down the main gully; after about 50 ft, when clean rock appears above, head straight up it and belay as soon as possible to avoid rope drag (or belay on the ledge itself). Another half pitch gains the upper SE ridge, from which you scramble around to the right to reach the top. The first-ascent party took 7-8 hours on the route and arrived at the summit after dark, bivying there.
overview: A committing, brushy Grade IV alpine rock route up Sperry's steep east face, climbing slabby rock beside a shrinking pocket glacier before working through a narrow, exposed jungle ledge and a final ridge scramble to the summit.

current.approach: When below the east face, scramble up through brush and easy rock to an obvious slabby rock face just left of the small pocket glacier on the east face.
current.descent: Not known in detail; parties would descend via the standard west-ridge/southwest-slope route to Lake Elan and out over Headlee Pass.
current.detailed_rack: A medium rock rack up to 4 inches with many extra runners for a wandering line.
current.pro_needs: Standard rack to 4" with plentiful slings/runners; natural pro (trees) supplements gear in the brushy sections.

name: Standard Scramble
beta: Hike the Sunrise Mine Trail from its trailhead through Wirtz Basin to Headlee Pass, traverse below Sperry's south ridge past Lake Elan (Vesper Lake), then scramble up slabs to the broad saddle between Sperry and Vesper Peaks. From the saddle, follow the west ridge/west slope upward -- easy at first, but above a down-sloping talus and heather bench the route steepens and the exposure increases into sustained Class 3-4 terrain to the summit. Many parties combine Sperry with adjacent Vesper Peak from the same saddle in one long day.
overview: Sperry Peak (6,120+ ft, USGS contour interval; some LIDAR-based lists cite ~6,140 ft) sits directly across the Sunrise Mine basin from Vesper Peak, rising over 3,900 ft above the South Fork Stillaguamish in about a mile. It's a straightforward-looking but sneaky Class 2-3 scramble on talus, heather benches and low-angle slab, with a loose, sustained, and routefinding-heavy final push to a small summit. Named for A. D. "Dick" Sperry, an 1890s Silverton mining prospector; first ascended in 1927 by Norval Grigg and Art Winder.

current.approach: From the Sunrise Mine Trailhead (2,350 ft, end of FS Road 4065), follow the Sunrise Mine Trail (#707) into the Morning Star NRCA. About 0.5 mile in, the trail makes a tricky crossing of the South Fork Stillaguamish River — no bridge, sometimes aided by a small-diameter log and a hand rope; this ford can be genuinely difficult and dangerous after heavy rain or early-season snowmelt. Beyond the crossing the trail climbs gradually through forest for roughly a mile to Wirtz Basin, where the terrain opens up and turns rockier. From the basin the trail steepens sharply into a narrow, loose rock chute switchbacking up to Headlee Pass (4,720 ft, about 2.7 miles from the trailhead) — this chute is notorious for rockfall dislodged by parties above and is also an avalanche path in shoulder-season/spring snow conditions, so groups should spread out and move through it deliberately. From Headlee Pass the trail contours around Sperry's south/east flank and drops slightly into the upper Vesper Creek basin to Vesper Lake (Lake Elan, roughly 3 miles in). Leave the maintained trail at the lake's outlet, follow its east shore, then climb open, welcoming slopes to the saddle/notch between Vesper and Sperry Peaks (Sperry Saddle). From the saddle it's off-trail scrambling up Sperry's west ridge/west slope — loose, often wet dirt and heather with class 3 rock steps, including some brushy, tree-assisted moves in the final push to the summit block — to the 6,120 ft summit. Total distance to the top is around 4 miles with roughly 3,700 ft of gain; water is available at the South Fork crossing and at Vesper Lake but not much beyond it, so top off before leaving the lake.
approach_variant_names: Headlee Pass and Lake Elan
current.descent: Reverse the ascent line: downclimb the loose, brushy west ridge/west slope scramble back to Sperry Saddle, then drop to the Vesper Lake outlet and rejoin the maintained Sunrise Mine Trail. Route-finding on the upper scramble is the main hazard on the way down — the easiest line up is not obvious from above, and it's easy to end up descending a different, steeper gully than the one you climbed, so note landmarks (the climber's-right ramp and the cairned dirt path into the trees) on the way up and look for them again on the way down. From the lake, retrace the trail back through Headlee Pass and down its rockfall-prone switchback chute (loose underfoot, stay alert for rock knocked loose by other parties), through Wirtz Basin, back across the South Fork Stillaguamish ford, and out to the trailhead. This is a walk-off/downclimb scramble route with no rappelling involved anywhere on the standard line.
current.detailed_rack: No technical rack.
current.pro_needs: None.
bivy: Sunrise Mine road end — the Sperry and Vesper Creek staging point
Red Bridge Campground, Mountain Loop Highway

name: Upper South Ridge
beta: Follows the standard approach to Headlee Pass, then crosses the talus toward Lake Elan/Vesper Lake and takes the first ramp up and right to the base of the South Ridge. The route climbs the ridgecrest with a brief detour onto its left side about halfway up: a ~200 ft, Class 4 first tower, then easier Class 2-3 climbing back to the ridgecrest, a 5th-class section (which is actually a downclimb off a block), then a couple more ropelengths of Class 3-4 to a false summit, and a couple more ropelengths beyond that to the true summit. Simul-climbing or moving unroped is recommended rather than pitching it out formally.
overview: A more technical, low-5th-class ridge scramble/climb on Sperry's south side - harder and more interesting than the standard route but without the commitment of the north/east face lines. It is heavily vegetated and not recommended for quality, though it is a real, documented line.

current.approach: Approach to Headlee Pass as for the standard route (see that route's approach). Cross the talus toward Vesper/Elan Lake, then take the first ramp heading up and to the right to reach the base of the South Ridge.
current.descent: From the summit, follow the standard Class 3 route down to the west to the pass between Vesper and Sperry, then head south back over Headlee Pass and down to the car - do not try to reverse the South Ridge itself.
current.detailed_rack: A light rack to 2 inches, long slings for slinging trees (substituting for gear in the brushy sections), and a short rope for simul-climbing.
current.pro_needs: Light trad rack to 2" supplemented heavily by slung trees; this is a simul-climb/scramble style ascent rather than a fully pitched-out route.

name: Southeast Gully / East Ridge (Spider-Formidable Col)
beta: From a high camp at Kool-Aid Lake or Spider-Formidable Col, cross the Middle Cascade Glacier to the col, descend briefly onto its south side, and traverse east under snow to a steep, narrow gully immediately right (east) of a central buttress on Spider's south/southeast face. The gully is choked with loose rock and has small Class 3 steps; most parties exit early onto the buttress (left) or a rib (right) rather than following it to its top. From the buttress/rib, gain the ridge east of the summit and traverse west (Class 3, staying south of the corniced crest) to the top. The rock is schist and notoriously rotten.
overview: The standard route: glacier travel and a talus approach to Spider-Formidable Col, then a loose, narrow southeast-facing gully and rock buttress up onto the east ridge, finishing with a short Class 3 traverse along a corniced arête to the summit.

current.approach: From the Cascade Pass Trailhead (3,600 ft, at the end of the 23.1-mile Cascade River Road from Marblemount), hike the Cascade Pass Trail 3.7 miles to Cascade Pass (~5,400-5,560 ft). Continue on a climbers' path across talus to Cache Col (~6,900 ft), then descend steep snowfields (ice axe/crampons often needed) into the Kool-Aid Lake basin (~6,800 ft), a common base camp. From Kool-Aid Lake, cross talus/scree east toward Spider's south face, reach the fringe of the Middle Cascade Glacier (~6,500 ft) after a steep, narrow sidehill traverse, and cross the glacier (crevasses present; rope recommended) to Spider-Formidable Col (~7,320 ft), an alternate, higher base camp used by many climbing parties.
approach_variant_names: Spider-Formidable col to the south face
current.descent: Avoid re-descending directly through the main gully; parties typically angle down a secondary gully or onto an adjacent rib and zig-zag back toward the col rather than reversing the crux line exactly, to reduce exposure to rockfall triggered from above. From Spider-Formidable Col, re-cross the Middle Cascade Glacier, re-ascend to Cache Col, and descend the snowfields/boot path back to Cascade Pass and the trailhead.
current.detailed_rack: A rope for the Middle Cascade Glacier crossing. Once off the glacier the gully/ridge is climbed unroped as a scramble by most parties — a light rock rack is optional, not standard.
current.pro_needs: This is primarily an unroped glacier-approach scramble rather than a pitched rock climb; the real protection needs are a helmet against rockfall and standard crevasse-rescue gear for the glacier, not a traditional rack.
bivy: Cache Col and the Cache Glacier shoulder

name: Standard Route
beta: An all off-trail alpine scramble of roughly 6 miles and about 5,000 ft of elevation gain from the FR63 roadside parking to the summit. Sustained bushwhacking and blowdown low down give way to a cliff-band bypass and a snow/scree gully, ending with an exposed, sometimes loose ridge scramble with two short sections of 4th/low-5th-class climbing where a rope is often carried. It is one of the least-climbed of the Everett-area Pin Peaks, and sees sparse recent traffic.
overview: Spire Mountain (6,213-6,218 ft) is a three-summited peak — Northwest, Central, and Southeast Spires — in the Wild Sky Wilderness of the Mount Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, about 7 miles northeast of Index and 4 miles north-northeast of Gunn Peak. It rises directly above the North Fork Skykomish River, on the west side of the range, not near Sultan Basin or the Sauk drainage/Monte Cristo group. One of the least-often-climbed of the 'Everett Pin Peaks,' Spire is reached by a long, entirely off-trail approach through brush and cliff bands and finishes on an airy summit ridge with a genuine, exposed Class 5 step that trips up parties expecting an easy Class 3 walk-up.

current.approach: Drive US-2 to Skykomish, then north on Beckler River Road (FR-65) for about 15 miles; turn left (west) onto FR-63 and follow it about 4.6 miles to where it crosses the North Fork Skykomish River again. Just past that bridge the road bends right over a small rise about a mile east of Galena (~1,150 ft); park at the unmarked roadside pullout there. Leave the road on the side away from the river and head directly, off-trail, up the steep, blowdown-choked slope toward Spire Mountain. There is no tread anywhere on the mountain: the line works around cliff bands at roughly 4,200-4,400 ft on the peak's north side, traverses southeast to about 5,400 ft below the summit spires, and gains the west/northwest ridge for the final scramble to the top. An older, historic alternate approach (Fred Beckey's original line) starts south of Index via the North Fork Skykomish River Road, which now dead-ends at a washout around mile 6, then follows the unmaintained Trout Creek Road south to reach the same ridge — a much brushier ~16-mile, ~7,000 ft round trip, longer than today's standard FR-63 approach. Straight off the parking pullout the first stretch is thick fern hiding deadfall, which is slow in the dark in July; after the first old logging road the going is easier.
approach_variant_names: North Fork Skykomish riverside to the northwest saddle
current.descent: Descend by reversing the ascent line: downclimb (or rappel/back off facing in) the short Class 5 step near 6,100 ft, then retrace the ridge and the off-trail descent back through the 5,400 ft traverse and the 4,200-4,400 ft cliff-band bypass back down to the FR-63 roadside pullout. Loose rock, brush, and the lack of a defined tread make the descent slow going — budget real time for it and avoid straying north or east into steeper terrain where permanent snow/ice and cliffs persist.
current.detailed_rack: A light scrambling rack is sufficient: a single 30m/100 ft rope, a handful of slings including two double-length (240cm) runners for wrapping horns/blocks as rappel anchors, and optionally a few small nuts or cams if the party wants protection on the short 4th/low-5th-class steps near the top. This is not a route that requires a full trad rack.
rack: Optional light rack: 2-3 small cams, a few nuts
Short 30m rope or hand line for the Class 5 step
current.pro_needs: No rack needed for a typical ascent — a short hand line or a light 30m rope is enough to protect the one Class 5 step near 6,100 ft.
bivy: Spire Mountain — the saddle northwest of the summit
current.rope_note: Spire Mountain near Index; ~6mi off-trail, 5,000ft gain, finishing on the west ridge. Mostly Class 3 with short Class 4/occasional Class 5 spots where a rope is sometimes used.
